practicalMissions.helpPromptTemplate: I am on Week {weekNumber}, Mission {missionNumber} of the XcelerateAI Bootcamp. I am trying to build {missionTitle}. I created these files: {filesCreated}. The error I got is: {errorMessage}. I have tried: {attempts}. Please help me debug this without giving me the full answer immediately.
practicalMissions.background: A 'toolchain' is the full chain of tools code passes through before you see a result - editor, terminal, runtime. Verifying it means proving every link works, not hoping it does.
hints: Run `node -v` and `npm -v` as two separate commands and read each output before moving on.
`first-run.js` only needs `console.log(...)` lines - resist adding anything more complex.
commonMistakes: Running `node -v` in a different terminal tab than `node first-run.js`, then being confused when results seem inconsistent.
debuggingChecklist: Confirm the terminal prompt shows you inside the project folder before running anything.
Re-run `node -v` alone if the file fails, to isolate whether Node or your file is the problem.
thinkingPrompts: If `node first-run.js` printed nothing, would that mean the file is empty, or that it errored before your first console.log?
practicalMissions.stretchChallenge: Add a line printing the current date via `new Date()`, and explain in the README what type of value that is.
practicalMissions.realWorldApplications: Every professional onboarding starts with exactly this: verify the toolchain before writing any product code.
practicalMissions.commanderNotes: Most learners rush this one. Don't. A verified toolchain is the cheapest insurance you'll buy all bootcamp.
practicalMissions.approachOutline: This mission has no program logic to design — it is a verification exercise. You are proving four independent links in a chain work: the editor opens the folder, Node reports a version, a .js file you wrote actually executes, and Git records it. Treat each as its own check with its own evidence, because when something fails later you need to know which link broke. first-run.js itself only needs console.log lines; resist adding logic it does not ask for.

practicalMissions.helpPromptTemplate: I am on Week {weekNumber}, Mission {missionNumber} of the XcelerateAI Bootcamp. I am trying to build {missionTitle}. I created these files: {filesCreated}. The error I got is: {errorMessage}. I have tried: {attempts}. Please help me debug this without giving me the full answer immediately.
practicalMissions.background: A 'mission log' here is just a structured console report - the same pattern you'll use later for API responses and debug output, with plain variables instead of network data.
hints: Template literals (`` `Hello ${name}` ``) read far better than chaining `+` between strings.
If a printed value shows `undefined`, the variable was declared but never assigned - or assigned after it printed.
commonMistakes: Believing a variable updates everywhere automatically after you change it once, rather than re-running the prints that reference it.
debuggingChecklist: Check for a missing closing quote or backtick on the exact line the error names.
Confirm every variable used in a print was declared above it, not below.
thinkingPrompts: Why might five separate single-purpose print lines be more debuggable than one giant combined string?
practicalMissions.stretchChallenge: Turn the five print lines into a single multi-line template literal report and compare readability.
practicalMissions.realWorldApplications: Structured status logging is exactly what you'll use to debug a backend server in Month 4 when there's no UI to look at.
practicalMissions.commanderNotes: The debugging drill here - deleting a quote on purpose - is the highest-value habit in this whole mission.
practicalMissions.approachOutline: Declare each piece of information as its own named variable, then build the printed lines from those variables rather than typing the text directly into console.log. The point of the mission is the link between a stored value and what appears on screen: when you change one variable and re-run, exactly one part of the output should change. If nothing changes, the value was hardcoded into the message instead of read from the variable.
practicalMissions.scopeNote: Unlike Mission 1.1, which only verified that tools work, this mission asks you to write actual program logic — values stored in variables and read back out.

practicalMissions.helpPromptTemplate: I am on Week {weekNumber}, Mission {missionNumber} of the XcelerateAI Bootcamp. I am trying to build {missionTitle}. I created these files: {filesCreated}. The error I got is: {errorMessage}. I have tried: {attempts}. Please help me debug this without giving me the full answer immediately.
practicalMissions.background: This mission has no new syntax - it exists purely to make 'proof of work' a habit, not an afterthought tacked onto the end of a project.
hints: A README doesn't need to be long - it needs to let a stranger run your code without asking one question.
`git status` before and after `git add`/`commit` is the fastest way to build intuition for what each command does.
commonMistakes: Writing a README that describes what the code does conceptually but never states the exact command to run it.
debuggingChecklist: Does your README include the literal `node filename.js` command, copy-pasteable?
Did `git status` show 'nothing to commit' after committing, confirming it saved?
thinkingPrompts: If you reopened this repo in a year with no memory of it, could your README alone get you running in under two minutes?
practicalMissions.stretchChallenge: Add a `.gitignore` file and explain in the README why it's there, even with nothing to ignore yet.
practicalMissions.realWorldApplications: Every employer and client reads your README and commit history before running your code - this is the actual first impression.
practicalMissions.commanderNotes: This is the smallest mission of the week and the one that matters most for your portfolio's first impression.
practicalMissions.approachOutline: There is no new syntax here. The deliverable is written, not coded: a README that lets a stranger reproduce your week without asking you anything, and a commit that proves the work exists. Write the README as instructions to someone who has never seen the folder, then follow your own instructions literally to find what you left out.
practicalMissions.scopeNote: This mission produces documentation and a commit rather than a running program — the previous two missions were code, this one is evidence.

If nothing changes, the value was hardcoded into the message instead of read from the variable.

_raw.briefing: Study, practice, prove, and reflect on Launch Environment and First JavaScript Output.
_raw.elliotConnection: Elliot begins as code you can run. This week proves you can create files, run JavaScript, read errors, and preserve work in GitHub.
_raw.scenario: Before Elliot can be a product, it has to be a file that runs. This week is about proving your machine is a real cockpit: you can create a file, make the computer execute it, read what it tells you back, and save that proof somewhere permanent. Every professional workflow you'll ever use - debugging, testing, deploying - depends on this loop working reliably first.
learningObjectives: Install and verify VS Code, Node.js, and Git
Use an integrated terminal inside VS Code
Create and run a JavaScript file with node
Read a terminal error and locate the line it points to
Initialize a Git repository and push a first commit
_raw.expectedOutcome: A GitHub repository containing at least two runnable JavaScript files and a README that explains, in your own words, how to set up and run them.
stretchGoals: Add a package.json with a `start` script so the project runs with `npm start`.
Write a version of first-run.js that reads a value from a command-line argument (`process.argv`).
hints: If `node -v` or `npm -v` prints nothing, the terminal you opened predates the install - close and reopen VS Code's terminal.
VS Code's integrated terminal starts in your open folder - you rarely need `cd` if you opened the right folder with `code .`.
`console.log` is not the only way to see a value - the bare Node REPL (`node` with no filename) prints any expression you type.
commonMistakes: Assuming a terminal error means the whole toolchain is broken, rather than reading which specific file and line it points to.
Believing 'the file exists in the folder' is the same as 'the terminal is currently inside that folder'.
Treating the first successful console.log as proof the setup is solid, without ever deliberately breaking something to see a real failure.
debugChecklist: Is the terminal's current folder the same folder the file is saved in?
Did you save the file before running it?
Is the exact filename typed correctly, including `.js`?
Does the error name a line number - have you opened that exact line?
Does `node -v` alone still work, confirming Node itself is fine?
thinkingPrompts: What actually happens when you type `node first-run.js` - what program reads your file, and what does it do with it?
If a teammate said 'it doesn't work,' what three questions would you ask before touching their code?
recallPrompts: Without looking it up, what command checks your installed Node.js version?
What is the difference between `git add` and `git commit`?
_raw.missionReview: This week had one real goal disguised as three missions: prove you can create, run, break, read, fix, and save code - reliably, not by luck. If you can already picture doing that loop again on a harder problem without panicking, Week 1 did its job.
_raw.progressNotes: Slow, careful terminal work now is what makes Month 4's backend server and Month 6's full Elliot assembly feel routine instead of terrifying - you're building muscle memory, not just a file.
_raw.missionDebrief: Environment confirmed. Toolchain verified. Your first commits are on GitHub and they will still be there in six months when Elliot V1 ships - that repository is now part of your permanent professional record.
_raw.commanderNotes: Every learner who finished this bootcamp started exactly where you are: a blank folder and a terminal that feels unfamiliar. The terminal stops feeling strange around week three. Keep the error messages - they're more useful than they feel right now.
_raw.nextMissionTeaser: Next week Elliot gets an identity: names, goals, and numbers stored in variables you control. The terminal skills you just built are about to start feeling routine.

_raw.briefing: Study, practice, prove, and reflect on Variables, Types, Strings, and Numbers.
_raw.elliotConnection: Elliot must know names, roles, goals, and project context. Variables and strings are the smallest building blocks of that memory.
_raw.scenario: Elliot's very first piece of real memory is small: a name, a role, a goal, a number of hours. Variables and types are how any program holds onto a fact instead of losing it the instant execution moves on. This week you build the smallest possible working memory system and prove you understand exactly what kind of value lives inside it.
learningObjectives: Declare variables with let and const and explain when to use each
Identify the type of any value
Use arithmetic operators to calculate derived values
Build multi-line output using template literals
Explain, with an example, what type coercion is and why it causes bugs
_raw.expectedOutcome: Three small working programs - a personal profile card, a real bootcamp-hours calculator, and a multi-line string report - each pushed to GitHub with a README.
stretchGoals: Add a variable holding an array of your goals and print its length in the profile report.
Use `typeof` on every variable in the Profile Data Card and print each type next to its value.
hints: `const` should be your default - reach for `let` only when a value genuinely needs to change.
If a calculation prints `NaN`, a number got treated as text somewhere upstream - trace backward to where the value was created.
commonMistakes: Believing `let` and `var` are interchangeable, when only `let`/`const` should be used.
Assuming a number in quotes (`"25"`) behaves like a real number (`25`) in a calculation.
Thinking a variable stores the expression used to create it, rather than the single computed value that resulted.
debugChecklist: Print the `typeof` of any value producing unexpected output.
Check whether a number came from input, a template literal, or concatenation - all can silently produce text.
Confirm every variable in a calculation is declared before it runs.
thinkingPrompts: If Elliot needs 'weekly hours' to calculate a six-month total, what type must it be, and what breaks if it were text?
Why might `const` reduce bugs compared to always defaulting to `let`?
recallPrompts: What are the three primitive types you used this week?
What symbol wraps an embedded expression inside a template literal?
_raw.missionReview: By now you've watched output change simply because a stored value changed - that's the entire point of variables, and the exact mechanism React state (Month 3) and a database record (Month 4) both build on.
_raw.progressNotes: If the hours math or template literals felt slower than Week 1, that's expected - you're doing real reasoning now, not just proving the toolchain works.
_raw.missionDebrief: Elliot's identity data now exists as real, typed, calculable information. Every later mission that says 'store the user's X' is a variant of exactly what you just built.
_raw.commanderNotes: If `NaN` showed up anywhere this week, good - it's the single most instructive bug in JavaScript, and you now know what causes it.
_raw.nextMissionTeaser: Next week, Elliot starts making decisions. Everything you stored this week becomes something a function can check and respond to.

practicalMissions.background: 'Readiness checking' is a real pattern - CI/CD pipelines, health-check endpoints, and onboarding flows all run a version of exactly this logic before allowing the next step.
hints: Write all four input combinations on paper and decide the correct output for each before writing the chain.
Order conditions most-specific/urgent first so an early match doesn't swallow a later one.
commonMistakes: Ordering conditions so a broad earlier one accidentally catches a case meant for a specific later one.
debuggingChecklist: Manually trace each of the four combinations line by line.
Confirm blockersOpen is compared as a number, not a string.
thinkingPrompts: If two conditions could both be true, which wins, and why did you order them that way?
practicalMissions.stretchChallenge: Add a 'Needs Review' level for when proof is submitted but a blocker is still open.
practicalMissions.realWorldApplications: This is the shape of logic that decides whether a pull request is allowed to merge in a real CI pipeline.
practicalMissions.approachOutline: This is a single script, not a set of functions. Declare the inputs as variables at the top, then write one if/else chain that resolves to exactly one of three outcomes: Ready, Almost Ready, or Blocked. The three facts you need to weigh are whether the required tasks are complete, whether any blockers are open, and whether proof was submitted. Deciding which of those should be tested first — and what that ordering does to cases where more than one is true at once — is the actual work of this mission, so it is deliberately left to you. Write out your four test combinations and their expected answers before you write the chain, then check the code against that list.
practicalMissions.scopeNote: Despite the week being titled "Conditionals and Functions," this specific mission uses conditionals only — you are not asked to declare any functions here. Functions arrive in Mission 3.2.

practicalMissions.background: These three small functions are a miniature version of exactly what Elliot's real assistant engine does in Month 6 - without a network request in between.
hints: Give each function one job - `getProgressStatus` should not also give blocker advice.
Test each function alone before combining outputs.
commonMistakes: Writing one large function that does everything, making it impossible to test a single piece.
debuggingChecklist: Call each function individually and log its raw return before combining.
Confirm every code path has an explicit `return`, including edge cases.
thinkingPrompts: If you reused `getBlockerAdvice` in a bigger program, would today's version work standalone, or does it secretly depend on something outside itself?
practicalMissions.stretchChallenge: Add `formatAssistantReply(status, advice, action)` that composes the other three into one paragraph.
practicalMissions.realWorldApplications: Composing small pure functions into one response is exactly how Elliot's Month 6 assistant engine is structured.
practicalMissions.approachOutline: Build three separate, independent functions. Each takes one plain value as a parameter — a percentage number, a blocker count, a week number — and returns a string; none of them share state or call each other. Get one working and tested on its own before writing the next. Only after all three return correct values do you combine their results into a single printed recommendation. The distinction that matters here is return versus print: a function that only console.logs cannot have its output reused by the code that called it.
practicalMissions.scopeNote: This mission has a different shape from Mission 3.1. That one was a single script branching over variables you declared at the top; this one needs three independent functions, each taking a plain value as a parameter and returning a string. Do not carry the previous mission's single-script structure into this one.

_raw.briefing: Study, practice, prove, and reflect on Conditionals and Functions.
_raw.elliotConnection: Elliot will need to decide how to respond: task due, progress low, goal active, note found, document uploaded. That starts with if-statements and functions.
_raw.scenario: An assistant that can only print is a script. An assistant that can decide is closer to a product. This week Elliot gets its first real decisions: given a situation (progress, blockers, deadline), what should it say back? Conditionals give it branches; functions give it reusable, testable logic instead of one tangled script.
learningObjectives: Write multi-branch decisions with if / else if / else
Distinguish a function declaration from an expression
Write functions that accept parameters and return a value
Explain why a returned value is more reusable than a printed one
Combine functions and conditionals into one decision flow
_raw.expectedOutcome: A working Elliot Response Engine that accepts different input combinations and returns different, correct, assistant-style advice for each.
stretchGoals: Add a fourth function that combines the other three's outputs into one formatted paragraph.
Replace one if/else chain with a switch statement and compare readability.
hints: Write the plain-English decision first before typing any code.
A function that only uses `console.log` and never `return`s is usually doing the caller's job for it.
commonMistakes: Using `=` where `===` was intended inside a condition - this week's drill exists to make that visible once.
Believing a function 'runs itself' when defined, without realizing it must be called.
Confusing what a function prints with what it returns.
debugChecklist: If a condition never triggers, check for a single `=` instead of `===`.
If a result is `undefined` where you expected a value, check for a missing `return`.
Trace a decision by hand with real values before assuming the logic is wrong.
thinkingPrompts: Given three outcomes (Ready / Almost Ready / Blocked), what is the minimum number of conditions to separate all three?
Why might returning a value be better than printing inside a reusable function?
recallPrompts: What is the difference between `=` and `===`?
Name one difference between a function declaration and a function expression.
_raw.missionReview: You've now written code that makes a real decision based on real conditions - the conceptual seed of every 'if the user is logged in, show X' pattern you'll write for the rest of the bootcamp.
_raw.progressNotes: If the Boss Drill took longer than the other two missions, that's expected - it deliberately combines everything from the whole week into one flow.
_raw.missionDebrief: Elliot can now reason about a situation and respond differently. That is, functionally, the smallest definition of 'intelligent behavior' - built from three plain functions and some if statements.
_raw.commanderNotes: The `=` vs `===` bug you triggered is one every professional has shipped to production at least once. Recognizing it fast is a real skill.
_raw.nextMissionTeaser: Next week, Elliot needs to hold more than one thing at a time - multiple goals, projects, notes. Arrays and objects are how real data collections get modeled.

practicalMissions.background: Arrays are the default shape for 'many of the same kind of thing' - and Elliot will hold arrays of notes, tasks, and documents by Month 4.
hints: A `for` loop's index starts at 0, but you can print `index + 1` for human-friendly numbering.
Adding a project is just pushing a string onto the same array - the loop that prints it doesn't change.
commonMistakes: Off-by-one errors - printing one too many or too few items because the stopping condition is slightly wrong.
debuggingChecklist: Log `projects.length` and compare against how many lines printed.
Confirm the loop variable indexes into the array, not just counts.
thinkingPrompts: If you needed to insert a project in the middle instead of the end, what would that require, and why is it different from adding to the end?
practicalMissions.stretchChallenge: Add a second array of 'completed projects' and print both lists with different headers.
practicalMissions.realWorldApplications: Rendering a numbered list from an array is exactly the operation React's `.map()` performs starting Week 11.
practicalMissions.approachOutline: Store the project names in a single array of strings, then let one loop do all the printing rather than writing a line per project. Prove the loop is genuinely driven by the array by adding a project and confirming the output grows without touching the loop.

practicalMissions.background: An object here plays the same role a database record will play in Month 4 - one structured entity with named fields, not a loose pile of variables.
hints: Access nested properties step by step (`userMemory.goals`, then `userMemory.goals[0]`) if a long chain confuses you.
Updating a property is a normal assignment - no special syntax needed.
commonMistakes: Reassigning the whole parent object instead of targeting the specific nested key.
debuggingChecklist: Log the full object before and after your update to confirm what changed.
Double-check property spelling and case against the object's definition.
thinkingPrompts: Why does representing projects as an array of objects make it easier to add a sixth project later than five separate variables would?
practicalMissions.stretchChallenge: Add a `notes` array inside each project object and print them nested under each project.
practicalMissions.realWorldApplications: This userMemory shape becomes the real JSON payload Elliot's backend sends and receives starting Week 14.
practicalMissions.approachOutline: Two structures work together here. One object holds the single user and their details; a separate array holds several project objects, each with its own properties. Build and print the user object first, then the projects array, then loop it to print a summary per project. Finally change one property in place and print again to confirm the object is genuinely mutable. When a printed value comes out undefined, compare the exact spelling of the key you read against the key you defined — that mismatch is silent in JavaScript.
practicalMissions.scopeNote: Where Mission 4.1 used an array of plain strings, this mission needs objects with named properties, and an array whose items are objects rather than text.

practicalMissions.background: This is the first mission that asks you to split a program across multiple files - a deliberate rehearsal for how every real project from Month 3 on is organized.
hints: Get it running in one file first if you're not confident splitting - then refactor into data.js/utils.js once it works.
Test each of the three required scenarios one at a time.
commonMistakes: Splitting files before the single-file version works, so you can't tell if a bug is in the logic or the file-splitting.
debuggingChecklist: Get the whole toolkit working as one file first, then split - never debug both at once.

thinkingPrompts: Across all twelve Month 1 missions, which concept do you feel least confident explaining out loud - and what would you build to test that gap?
practicalMissions.stretchChallenge: Add a command-line argument (`process.argv`) that lets you choose which scenario to run without editing the file.
practicalMissions.realWorldApplications: A multi-file, single-purpose structure is the direct ancestor of every React and Node project you'll build for the rest of the bootcamp.
practicalMissions.commanderNotes: Your Month 1 graduation project. If you can explain every file in this toolkit out loud, you are genuinely ready for the browser.
practicalMissions.approachOutline: This is an integration mission: nothing new, everything together. The intended split is data in one file, reusable helper functions in another, and a third that pulls them together to produce the report. Build it working as a single file first if the module syntax is unfamiliar, then split — debugging broken logic and broken imports simultaneously is far harder than doing them in sequence. The final report should draw on all four weeks: values in variables, decisions from conditionals, reusable helpers, and collections held in arrays and objects.

_raw.briefing: Study, practice, prove, and reflect on Arrays, Objects, Loops, and Month 1 Boss.
_raw.elliotConnection: Elliot needs structured knowledge. Arrays and objects let you store many notes, projects, and resources in a format code can search and display.
concepts: Combining arrays, objects, functions, and conditionals
_raw.scenario: A real assistant doesn't manage one goal or project - it manages many, in a structure it can search and update. This week Elliot gets a real memory shape: arrays for lists, objects for the details of any one thing, and loops for processing all of them without repeating code. The Month 1 Boss asks you to prove all four weeks work together in one program.
learningObjectives: Create and iterate over arrays with loops
Create objects with multiple properties and access by key
Access and update nested properties
Combine arrays of objects to represent a real collection
Assemble variables, conditionals, functions, arrays, and objects into one multi-file program
_raw.expectedOutcome: A Personal JavaScript Toolkit - a working, multi-file command-line program using every Month 1 concept together to report on your own goals and projects.
stretchGoals: Add a `filter` or `find` call to search the projects array by status.
Add a second nested object (e.g., `settings`) inside userMemory and access a value two levels deep.
hints: Build the array first and confirm the loop prints every item before adding objects to it.
Accessing a missing property returns `undefined` silently, which is often more confusing than an error.
commonMistakes: Confusing an array's index (position) with a value stored inside it.
Relying on object property order for meaning, when order should never carry meaning.
Misspelling a property key on read, getting `undefined`, and mistaking it for missing data rather than a typo.
debugChecklist: If a loop skips the last item, check `<` vs `<=` against the array length.
If a property read is `undefined`, compare exact spelling and case to where it was defined.
Print the whole object with `console.log(obj)` before accessing one nested piece.
thinkingPrompts: Why is an array right for 'a list of projects' while an object is right for 'the details of one project'?
What goes wrong if you model a list of projects with only separate variables, like Week 2 did for one profile?
recallPrompts: How do you access the third item in an array called `projects`?
What are the two ways to access a property on an object?

months.description: The first month is where 'I understand code in theory' becomes 'I can make a computer do what I say, on my own machine, with my own hands.' You will not touch a database, a framework, or a phone this month - deliberately. Every mission strips away everything except the language itself: variables, decisions, functions, and the two data shapes (arrays and objects) that every later layer of Elliot is built from. If Month 1 goes well, nothing in Months 2-6 will feel like starting over; it will feel like adding a new room onto a foundation you already trust.
learningOutcome: Set up and verify a professional local development environment from scratch
Write, run, and debug JavaScript programs using the terminal and VS Code
Model real information (identity, goals, projects) using variables, strings, and numbers
Make a program branch and decide using conditionals and functions
Store and process collections of structured data using arrays, objects, and loops
Push every unit of work to GitHub with a README a stranger could follow
months.milestoneDescription: By the end of Month 1 you will have shipped a Personal JavaScript Toolkit - a multi-file command-line program that models your own goals and projects and reports on them - built entirely from concepts introduced this month, with zero copied solutions.
months.motivation: Every professional JavaScript developer, backend engineer, and mobile developer still writes this exact vocabulary - variables, conditionals, functions, arrays, objects - every single day. Nothing here is 'beginner code' that gets replaced later; it is the permanent alphabet everything else in this bootcamp is written in.
months.recommendedPreparation: Have your laptop charged, a notebook for errors and commands, and your GitHub account ready before Week 1 begins. No prior JavaScript-specific experience is assumed - only comfort with what code, apps, and deployment are in theory.
months.careerInsight: In interviews for junior full-stack roles, the fundamentals in this month (closures, array methods, type coercion, `==` vs `===`) are the single most commonly tested topic. Mastering them now pays off at every hiring stage later.

What the mission asks for:
- Run all test cases.
- Create one intentional bug and fix it.
- Add a Commander Mode improvement if time allows.
- Write proof in README.

The concepts this mission is meant to exercise are: Systematic verification against test cases, Controlled failure and recovery, Documenting a fix.

Intended approach:
Work the loop deliberately: run every test case and record the result, break exactly one thing on purpose, observe precisely how the failure presents, then repair it and write down what the symptom was and what caused it. Breaking one thing at a time is what makes the symptom attributable — several simultaneous changes teach nothing.

Important scope note: This mission verifies and documents the work from earlier in the week rather than building anything new.

I have not written any code yet — I want to understand what is being asked before I start.

Please help me understand the requirements and plan my approach. Stay strictly inside the concepts listed above, even if a more complete or more advanced solution occurs to you: going beyond that scope makes this harder for me to learn from, not easier. Do not write the solution for me, and do not introduce techniques the mission did not ask for.

Which was more natural for your layout - Flexbox or Grid - and why?
How does building this landing card by hand change how you expect React components to work later?
What did resizing the browser to phone width reveal that desktop width hid?
What part of this interface are you most proud of, and what would you improve with more time?

_raw.briefing: Study, practice, prove, and reflect on HTML/CSS Interface Structure.
_raw.elliotConnection: Elliot cannot remain a terminal script. It needs an interface. This week creates the visual layer of your future assistant.
concepts: CSS selectors and the box model
_raw.scenario: Elliot cannot remain a terminal script - a product needs an interface a human wants to look at. This week builds Elliot's visual layer: a landing card with a hero and project cards that reads well on both a laptop and your Samsung A70's screen.
learningObjectives: Structure a page with semantic HTML sections
Style elements with CSS selectors and the box model
Lay out cards with Flexbox or Grid
Make a layout readable at phone width
Correctly link an external stylesheet
_raw.expectedOutcome: An Elliot Landing Card page - hero, call-to-action, and project cards for Portfolio, TheScoreboard, Growth OS, and Elliot - styled and mobile-readable, pushed to GitHub.
stretchGoals: Add a simple hover effect to the project cards using CSS `:hover`.
Use CSS custom properties (variables) for the XcelerateAI colors instead of repeating hex codes.
hints: A broken stylesheet link is silent - the page just renders unstyled. Check the `<link href>` path first when styles 'don't work'.
Flexbox is for one-dimensional rows/columns; Grid is for two-dimensional layouts. Cards in a row = Flexbox is usually simpler.
commonMistakes: Believing styles 'aren't applying' when really the CSS file is linked with a wrong path and never loads at all.
Using non-semantic `<div>` for everything instead of `<header>`, `<main>`, `<section>` - which hurts accessibility and readability.
Designing only at desktop width and never resizing the browser to check phone width.
debugChecklist: Is the `<link rel="stylesheet" href="...">` path correct relative to the HTML file?
Did you save both files before refreshing?
Does the browser DevTools 'Elements' tab show your CSS rules on the element, or are they crossed out/absent?
Have you resized the browser narrow to test mobile width?
Is a typo in a CSS property name silently ignoring the whole rule?
thinkingPrompts: Why does the browser render an unstyled page instead of throwing an error when the CSS link is broken?
Which parts of this landing card will need to become reusable components when you rebuild it in React?
recallPrompts: What HTML tag links an external stylesheet?
What is the difference between Flexbox and Grid in one sentence?
_raw.missionReview: You moved from output that only you see in a terminal to an interface anyone can open in a browser. That shift - invisible logic to visible product - is the whole point of Month 2.
_raw.progressNotes: HTML/CSS can feel less 'real' than JavaScript, but every product's first impression is its interface. Time spent here is not a detour from Elliot; it's Elliot's face.
_raw.missionDebrief: Elliot now has a visible identity. The exact hero-and-cards structure you built by hand this week is what you'll rebuild - faster and reusable - as React components in Month 3.
_raw.commanderNotes: Don't chase pixel-perfection this week. Chase 'clean, readable, and works on my phone.' Polish is a Month 5 concern; structure is this week's.
_raw.nextMissionTeaser: Next week the page stops being static - you'll reach into it with JavaScript and change its text on the fly using the DOM.

practicalMissions.helpPromptTemplate: I am on Week {weekNumber}, Mission {missionNumber} of the XcelerateAI Bootcamp. I am trying to build {missionTitle}. I created these files: {filesCreated}. The error I got is: {errorMessage}. I have tried: {attempts}. Please help me debug this without giving me the full answer immediately.
practicalMissions.background: This drill isolates the one thing that breaks most beginners' first DOM code: getting querySelector to actually find the element you mean.
hints: Give the elements you'll change clear, specific ids so the selector is unambiguous.
Log the result of querySelector immediately to confirm it isn't null before doing anything with it.
commonMistakes: Selecting an element that the script runs before the browser has created.
debuggingChecklist: Log each querySelector result.
Confirm ids in HTML match the selectors exactly.
thinkingPrompts: What's the safest place to put your `<script>` so every element it targets already exists?
practicalMissions.stretchChallenge: Select and update three different elements from a single script and confirm all three change.
practicalMissions.realWorldApplications: Live-updating on-page values is the backbone of dashboards, trackers, and status displays everywhere.
practicalMissions.approachOutline: Give the elements whose text will change a stable id or class in the HTML first, so the JavaScript has something reliable to target. Then select each one and write new text into it. Confirm a selector actually found something before using it — a selector that matches nothing returns null silently, and the error only appears when you try to use the result. Script placement matters: code that runs before the elements exist cannot find them.
practicalMissions.scopeNote: This week adds JavaScript back on top of last week's HTML and CSS — the page is no longer static, but the script now runs in the browser rather than in the terminal.

practicalMissions.background: The Status Panel is Elliot's first 'living' surface - values that JavaScript owns and updates, not text frozen in HTML.
hints: Store the status values in JS variables first, then write them into the DOM - don't hard-code them in the HTML.
A 'Last Updated' line is a tiny feature that makes the panel feel real - use `new Date().toLocaleTimeString()`.
commonMistakes: Hard-coding the status text in HTML and only pretending JavaScript set it - defeating the whole exercise.
Leaving console errors unresolved because 'the page still looks fine'.
debuggingChecklist: Confirm every displayed value originates from a JS variable, not the HTML.
Check the console is completely clear of errors.
thinkingPrompts: If the status came from a server instead of a variable, what part of this code would change and what would stay the same?
practicalMissions.stretchChallenge: Add a button that advances the mission status and updates the 'Last Updated' time each click.
practicalMissions.realWorldApplications: This is the literal pattern behind every 'Order status: Shipped' or 'Build: Passing' badge you've seen.
practicalMissions.commanderNotes: The test 'every value comes from JavaScript, not hard-coded HTML' is the real bar here. Hold yourself to it honestly.
practicalMissions.approachOutline: Extend the warm-up panel with a last-updated line, and treat a clean console as a requirement rather than a nicety. Each value that changes should be written through its own selector so a failure points at one field, not the whole panel.

practicalMissions.approachOutline: Run every test case, then deliberately break one selector so you can see exactly how a failed match presents in the console, and repair it. practicalMissions.background: This drill isolates the one thing that breaks most beginners' first DOM code: getting querySelector to actually find the element you mean.
hints: Give the elements you'll change clear, specific ids so the selector is unambiguous.
Log the result of querySelector immediately to confirm it isn't null before doing anything with it.
commonMistakes: Selecting an element that the script runs before the browser has created.
debuggingChecklist: Log each querySelector result.
Confirm ids in HTML match the selectors exactly.
thinkingPrompts: What's the safest place to put your `<script>` so every element it targets already exists?
practicalMissions.stretchChallenge: Select and update three different elements from a single script and confirm all three change.
practicalMissions.realWorldApplications: Live-updating on-page values is the backbone of dashboards, trackers, and status displays everywhere.
practicalMissions.approachOutline: Give the elements whose text will change a stable id or class in the HTML first, so the JavaScript has something reliable to target. Then select each one and write new text into it. Confirm a selector actually found something before using it — a selector that matches nothing returns null silently, and the error only appears when you try to use the result. Script placement matters: code that runs before the elements exist cannot find them.
practicalMissions.scopeNote: This week adds JavaScript back on top of last week's HTML and CSS — the page is no longer static, but the script now runs in the browser rather than in the terminal.

practicalMissions.background: Breaking a selector on purpose and fixing the resulting null is the most valuable DOM debugging rep you can do.
hints: A `null` error usually traces back to a selector that matched nothing - start there.
Document the exact wrong selector and the fix in your README.
commonMistakes: Fixing the null error without understanding that querySelector returned null in the first place.
debuggingChecklist: Run each test case for the week.
Confirm no console errors remain after the fix.
thinkingPrompts: What's the difference in the error you get from a null element vs. a typo'd property?
practicalMissions.stretchChallenge: Add a Commander Mode improvement such as color-coding the status text by state.
practicalMissions.realWorldApplications: 'Cannot read property of null' is one of the most common JS runtime errors in production - this drill inoculates you against it.
practicalMissions.approachOutline: Run every test case, then deliberately break one selector so you can see exactly how a failed match presents in the console, and repair it. A selector that matches nothing does not throw where it is written — it throws later, where the result is used. Recognising that gap is the point of the drill.

_raw.briefing: Study, practice, prove, and reflect on DOM Selection and Dynamic Text.
_raw.elliotConnection: A real assistant interface must respond to the user. DOM events are the first step toward chat buttons, task actions, and dashboard controls.
concepts: The DOM as a tree of nodes
Running JS after the page loads
_raw.scenario: A static page can't be an assistant. This week Elliot's interface comes alive: JavaScript reaches into the page, finds specific elements, and changes their text on the fly. This is the exact mechanism behind every status update, every live counter, and every dynamic label you've ever seen in an app.
learningObjectives: Explain the DOM as a tree the browser builds from your HTML
Select elements reliably with querySelector
Change an element's text from JavaScript
Display live status values (mission, project, status)
Run script code at the right time relative to page load
_raw.expectedOutcome: An Elliot Status Panel that displays current mission, active project, and status - with the text set dynamically by JavaScript, not hard-coded in HTML - and a 'Last Updated' line.
stretchGoals: Add a button that cycles the status through several values.
Show the real current time in the 'Last Updated' line using `new Date()`.
hints: If `querySelector` returns `null`, the selector doesn't match anything - check the exact id/class spelling in the HTML.
A `#` prefix selects by id, a `.` prefix selects by class - mixing these up is the most common selector bug.
commonMistakes: Running DOM code before the element exists (script above the HTML it targets), so querySelector returns null.
Confusing `textContent` (safe, plain text) with `innerHTML` (parses HTML, riskier).
Selecting by the wrong prefix - `#` vs `.` - and getting null.
debugChecklist: Did querySelector return null? Log it to confirm.
Does the selector prefix match (id needs #, class needs .)?
Is the script running after the target element exists in the DOM?
Is the id/class spelled identically in HTML and JS?
Are there console errors pointing at the failing line?
thinkingPrompts: Why does the browser turn your HTML into a tree of objects instead of just displaying the text directly?
When Elliot eventually chats, how is 'add a new message to the screen' just a bigger version of what you did this week?
recallPrompts: What does querySelector return when nothing matches?
What is the difference between selecting with `#` and with `.`?
_raw.missionReview: You made a web page change because your JavaScript told it to. Every interactive product is just this - selection plus modification - repeated at scale.
_raw.progressNotes: The DOM is the single most important browser concept in this bootcamp. React (Month 3) exists specifically to make what you did this week easier - so this week is what makes React click.
_raw.missionDebrief: Elliot's interface can now display live, JavaScript-driven data. Next week it will respond to the user, not just show information at them.
_raw.commanderNotes: If querySelector returning null frustrated you this week, good - that specific frustration is where real DOM intuition comes from.
_raw.nextMissionTeaser: Next week the page starts listening: buttons, clicks, and events turn your status panel into something the user can actually control.

commonMistakes: Running DOM code before the element exists (script above the HTML it targets), so querySelector returns null.
Confusing `textContent` (safe, plain text) with `innerHTML` (parses HTML, riskier).
Selecting by the wrong prefix - `#` vs `.` - and getting null.
debugChecklist: Did querySelector return null? Log it to confirm.
Does the selector prefix match (id needs #, class needs .)?
Is the script running after the target element exists in the DOM?
Is the id/class spelled identically in HTML and JS?
Are there console errors pointing at the failing line?
thinkingPrompts: Why does the browser turn your HTML into a tree of objects instead of just displaying the text directly?
When Elliot eventually chats, how is 'add a new message to the screen' just a bigger version of what you did this week?
recallPrompts: What does querySelector return when nothing matches?
What is the difference between selecting with `#` and with `.`?
weeks.missionReview: You made a web page change because your JavaScript told it to. Every interactive product is just this - selection plus modification - repeated at scale.
weeks.progressNotes: The DOM is the single most important browser concept in this bootcamp. React (Month 3) exists specifically to make what you did this week easier - so this week is what makes React click.
weeks.missionDebrief: Elliot's interface can now display live, JavaScript-driven data. Next week it will respond to the user, not just show information at them.
weeks.commanderNotes: If querySelector returning null frustrated you this week, good - that specific frustration is where real DOM intuition comes from.
weeks.nextMissionTeaser: Next week the page starts listening: buttons, clicks, and events turn your status panel into something the user can actually control.

practicalMissions.background: This drill isolates the single most misunderstood line in early JavaScript: attaching a handler correctly with addEventListener.
hints: Add a console.log inside the handler first, so you can confirm it fires before adding real logic.
Attach all three listeners before testing, then click each once.
commonMistakes: Writing `button.addEventListener('click', handler())` - the `()` runs it immediately instead of on click.
debuggingChecklist: Confirm you passed `handler`, not `handler()`.
Confirm the button element is non-null.
thinkingPrompts: If a listener runs once at page load instead of on click, what does that tell you about how you attached it?

practicalMissions.realWorldApplications: Every button, toggle, and menu in every app is an event listener - this is foundational, reused daily.
practicalMissions.approachOutline: Build the buttons in HTML, select each in JavaScript, then attach a listener to each one. The shift this week is that code no longer runs top to bottom once; it waits and responds.

_raw.briefing: Study, practice, prove, and reflect on DOM Events and Interactive UI.
_raw.elliotConnection: Elliot must save notes, goals, reminders, and tasks. This week builds the first memory pattern using browser storage.
concepts: Updating UI in response to actions
_raw.scenario: An assistant that only displays information isn't interactive - it's a poster. This week Elliot's interface starts responding: buttons that change status, mark progress, and confirm completion. Event listeners are the first step toward chat send buttons, task toggles, and every control Elliot will eventually have.
learningObjectives: Explain what a DOM event is and when it fires
Attach behavior to buttons with addEventListener
Update text and styles in response to a click
Show a success state after an action
Disable or change a control after it's used
_raw.expectedOutcome: A Bootcamp Status Board with Start / Learning / Completed buttons that update the status text and style on click, show a success message when completed, and disable the complete button afterward.
stretchGoals: Add a 'reset' button that returns the board to its starting state.
Track how many times each button was clicked and display the counts.
hints: `addEventListener('click', fn)` takes the function itself - don't call it with `fn()` (which runs it immediately once).
If a button 'does nothing,' confirm the listener attached to a real, non-null element.
commonMistakes: Passing `handler()` instead of `handler` to addEventListener, so it runs once at setup and never on click.
Attaching a listener to an element that querySelector didn't actually find (null).
Updating the text but forgetting to also update the visual state (class) so the UI looks inconsistent.
debugChecklist: Did you pass the function reference (`fn`) not the call (`fn()`)?
Is the element the listener is attached to actually non-null?
Is the event type spelled correctly ('click')?
Does the handler run at all? Add a console.log inside it.
Are text and style both updated together?
thinkingPrompts: Why does addEventListener take a function you don't call yourself?
How is a 'Mark Completed' button the same shape of problem as a chat 'Send' button?
recallPrompts: What's the difference between passing `fn` and `fn()` to addEventListener?
Name two things a click handler might change on the page.
_raw.missionReview: Your interface now reacts to the user. Display plus events equals interactivity - and interactivity is the difference between a page and an app.
_raw.progressNotes: Events are where beginners most often confuse 'define a function' with 'call a function.' If that clicked for you this week, a lot of React (which passes handlers as props) will feel familiar.
_raw.missionDebrief: Elliot's interface is now interactive. Next week it gains memory - the inputs users give it will survive a page refresh.
_raw.commanderNotes: The `fn` vs `fn()` distinction you practiced this week is one of the most common real bugs in React event handlers too. You're learning it early on purpose.
_raw.nextMissionTeaser: Next week: forms and localStorage. Elliot finally remembers what you tell it, even after you close the tab.

practicalMissions.approachOutline: Read the value out of the form, stop the browser's default submit from reloading the page, then persist the notes as a single array rather than as many separate keys. localStorage only holds strings, so the array has to be serialised on the way in and parsed on the way back out — skipping either step is what produces the "[object Object]" result. Verify persistence by actually refreshing, not by checking the value in memory.

practicalMissions.background: The Notes Vault is Elliot's first persistent memory and Month 2's flagship build - capture, store, render, delete, survive refresh.
hints: Re-render the whole notes list from localStorage after every change - simpler and less bug-prone than patching the DOM by hand.
Reject empty notes before saving; validating input is a core product habit, not an extra.
commonMistakes: Rendering notes only on save but not reloading them on page load, so a refresh appears to lose them.
Allowing empty notes to be saved, cluttering the list.
debuggingChecklist: Reload the page - do all notes reappear?
Does deleting one note leave the others intact and persisted?
Are empty submissions rejected?
thinkingPrompts: When Elliot's notes move to a backend in Month 4, which parts of this code stay and which get replaced by a fetch call?
practicalMissions.stretchChallenge: Add categories (learned / confused / next action) and let the user filter the list by category.
practicalMissions.realWorldApplications: A persistent notes list is a complete, useful micro-product - and the exact pattern behind todo apps, journals, and CRMs.
practicalMissions.commanderNotes: This is the mission that proves Month 2. When your notes survive a refresh, Elliot officially has memory. Don't move on until deletion and refresh both work cleanly.
practicalMissions.approachOutline: Extend the warm-up with rendering, deletion, and rejection of empty input. Keep one function responsible for drawing the list from storage and call it after every change, rather than editing the page directly in each handler — that single path is what keeps what is displayed and what is stored from drifting apart. Deletion must remove the item from the stored array and re-save, not merely remove it from the screen.

hints: Save, then immediately reload and load - if the notes come back, the round-trip works.

practicalMissions.approachOutline: Read the value out of the form, stop the browser's default submit from reloading the page, then persist the notes as a single array rather than as many separate keys. localStorage only holds strings, so the array has to be serialised on the way in and parsed on the way back out — skipping either step is what produces the "[object Object]" result. Verify persistence by actually refreshing, not by checking the value in memory.
practicalMissions.scopeNote: This is the first mission where data outlives the page — until now everything was lost on refresh.

_raw.briefing: Study, practice, prove, and reflect on Forms and localStorage.
_raw.elliotConnection: Elliot, TheScoreboard, and mobile apps all depend on structured data moving between frontend and backend. JSON and fetch are the bridge.
concepts: Rendering a saved list and deleting items
_raw.scenario: This is the week Elliot starts to remember. A form captures notes, localStorage saves them as JSON, and the notes survive a page refresh. This is Elliot's first real memory - the same read/write/persist pattern that every later notes, tasks, and knowledge feature is built on.
learningObjectives: Capture input values from a form
Prevent a form from reloading the page on submit
Save and load an array in localStorage using JSON
Render a saved list back to the page
Delete individual items and prevent empty entries
_raw.expectedOutcome: The Elliot Notes Vault: a browser app that saves notes to localStorage, renders them in a list, deletes individual notes, prevents empty notes, and keeps everything after a page refresh.
stretchGoals: Add note categories (learned / confused / next action) and filter by them.
Add an edit function that updates an existing note in place.
hints: localStorage only stores strings - you must `JSON.stringify` before saving and `JSON.parse` after loading.
A form submit reloads the page by default - call `event.preventDefault()` or your data vanishes instantly.
commonMistakes: Storing an object/array directly in localStorage without JSON.stringify, so it saves as the useless string '[object Object]'.
Forgetting preventDefault, so the page reloads on submit and appears to 'lose' the note.
Rendering notes once but not re-rendering after a save or delete.
debugChecklist: Are you JSON.stringify-ing before saving and JSON.parse-ing after loading?
Did you call event.preventDefault() on submit?
Does the notes array re-render after every save and delete?
Check localStorage in DevTools 'Application' tab - is the data actually there and valid JSON?
Are empty notes being rejected before save?
thinkingPrompts: Why does localStorage force you through JSON.stringify/parse instead of just storing your array directly?
How is this save/load/render loop the same one Elliot's backend will use in Month 4, just with a server instead of the browser?
recallPrompts: What two JSON functions convert between an object and a string?
What does event.preventDefault() stop from happening on a form submit?
_raw.missionReview: Elliot can now remember. The capture-store-render-persist cycle you built this week is the exact conceptual shape of every data feature for the rest of the bootcamp - it just moves to a server in Month 4.
_raw.progressNotes: This is the Month 2 boss week. If notes survive a refresh and you can explain why JSON.stringify was necessary, you've internalized browser persistence - a genuinely product-grade skill.
_raw.missionDebrief: Month 2 is complete: Elliot has an interface, responds to the user, and remembers data across sessions. Month 3 rebuilds all of this - faster and reusable - with React.
_raw.commanderNotes: The Notes Vault is your Month 2 flagship. When it survives a refresh with your notes intact, you've built Elliot's first real memory. That's a milestone worth screenshotting.
_raw.nextMissionTeaser: Month 3 begins with GitHub discipline and deployment, then introduces React - the tool that turns everything you built by hand this month into reusable components.

months.description: Month 2 takes everything you can already do in a terminal and gives it a face. Elliot stops being text scrolling past in a console and becomes something you can see, click, and interact with in a browser. You'll structure interfaces with HTML, style them with CSS, make them respond to the user with the DOM and events, and - critically - make them remember data between page refreshes with localStorage. By the end, Elliot has its first real interface and its first browser-based memory.
learningOutcome: Structure a web interface with semantic HTML and style it responsively with CSS
Select and modify page elements dynamically using the DOM
Make a page respond to user actions with events and event listeners
Capture user input through forms and validate it
Persist structured data in the browser with localStorage and JSON
months.milestoneDescription: By the end of Month 2 you will have shipped the Elliot Notes Vault: a browser app that captures notes through a form, saves them to localStorage, renders them back, and survives a page refresh - the first version of Elliot that remembers anything.
months.motivation: Every product a user actually touches is a DOM being manipulated by JavaScript in response to events. React (Month 3) is a faster way to do exactly what you'll do by hand this month - so doing it by hand once is what makes React make sense later instead of feeling like magic.
months.recommendedPreparation: Be fluent with Month 1's variables, functions, arrays, objects, and loops - the DOM is just those same tools pointed at a web page instead of a console.
months.careerInsight: 'Explain what the DOM is and how event delegation works' is a near-universal front-end interview question. The hands-on DOM work this month is where that answer comes from.

practicalMissions.background: The stage/unstage/commit cycle is the atomic unit of professional version control - this drill makes it deliberate rather than magical.
hints: Run `git status` at each step to watch the file move between untracked, staged, and committed.
Practice `git restore --staged <file>` to unstage without losing your work.
commonMistakes: Using `git add .` blindly without checking what it staged.
debuggingChecklist: Confirm `git status` reflects each stage/unstage.
Confirm the final commit contains exactly the intended file.
thinkingPrompts: Why does Git separate 'staging' from 'committing' at all?
practicalMissions.stretchChallenge: Make a commit, then practice `git log` to read your own history back.
practicalMissions.realWorldApplications: Precise staging is how professionals craft clean, reviewable pull requests.
futureConcepts: Branching and PRs (team work beyond bootcamp)
practicalMissions.approachOutline: This mission organises rather than builds. Give the repository a folder per week, add a log file for commits and one for bugs, and write a README that explains what the repository is to someone arriving cold. The staging drill matters: create a file, stage it, unstage it, then stage and commit it — watching git status between each step is what turns the staging area from an abstraction into something you can see.
practicalMissions.scopeNote: This week produces repository structure and written records rather than an application — there is nothing to run in a browser.

practicalMissions.background: The stage/unstage/commit cycle is the atomic unit of professional version control - this drill makes it deliberate rather than magical.
hints: Run `git status` at each step to watch the file move between untracked, staged, and committed.
Practice `git restore --staged <file>` to unstage without losing your work.
commonMistakes: Using `git add .` blindly without checking what it staged.
debuggingChecklist: Confirm `git status` reflects each stage/unstage.
Confirm the final commit contains exactly the intended file.
thinkingPrompts: Why does Git separate 'staging' from 'committing' at all?
practicalMissions.stretchChallenge: Make a commit, then practice `git log` to read your own history back.
practicalMissions.realWorldApplications: Precise staging is how professionals craft clean, reviewable pull requests.
futureConcepts: Branching and PRs (team work beyond bootcamp)
practicalMissions.approachOutline: This mission organises rather than builds. Give the repository a folder per week, add a log file for commits and one for bugs, and write a README that explains what the repository is to someone arriving cold. The staging drill matters: create a file, stage it, unstage it, then stage and commit it — watching git status between each step is what turns the staging area from an abstraction into something you can see.
practicalMissions.scopeNote: This week produces repository structure and written records rather than an application — there is nothing to run in a browser.

_raw.briefing: Study, practice, prove, and reflect on GitHub Workflow and Project Discipline.
_raw.elliotConnection: If it is not saved, versioned, and shareable, it is not proof. This week turns practice into public evidence.
_raw.scenario: If it isn't saved, versioned, and shareable, it isn't proof. This week turns your practice into a public professional record: a clean repo, meaningful commits, a bug log, and - ideally - a deployed live link. This is the discipline that makes everything after it demonstrable to an employer.
learningObjectives: Stage, unstage, and commit changes deliberately
Write commit messages that explain intent
Structure a repository a stranger can navigate
Maintain a commit log and bug log
Deploy a static project to a live URL
_raw.expectedOutcome: A GitHub Mission Protocol repo with a clean structure, a README explaining the bootcamp, a commit log, a bug log, and at least three well-messaged commits - ideally with one project deployed live.
stretchGoals: Deploy a previous Month 2 project (the Notes Vault) to Vercel or Netlify and add the live link to its README.
Add a simple GitHub profile README describing your bootcamp journey.
hints: `git status` before every commit shows exactly what you're about to save - make it a reflex.
A good commit message finishes the sentence 'This commit will...' - e.g., 'add delete button to notes vault'.
commonMistakes: Vague commit messages ('fix', 'update', 'final v2') that make the history unreadable as a portfolio.
Committing everything in one giant commit instead of small, logical ones.
Never deploying, so the portfolio has no live, clickable evidence.
debugChecklist: Does `git status` show only the files you intend to commit?
Is each commit message specific about what changed?
Does the README let a stranger run the project?
If deployed, does the live URL actually load the current version?
Are secrets/keys kept out of the repo?
thinkingPrompts: What does an employer learn about you from your commit history in the first thirty seconds?
Why is a small, well-messaged commit more valuable than one giant 'done' commit?
recallPrompts: What command shows what you're about to commit?
What makes a commit message useful to your future self?
_raw.missionReview: Your work is now public, structured, and (ideally) live. This is the difference between 'I learned to code' and 'here is proof I can build and ship.'
_raw.progressNotes: Deployment can feel intimidating the first time and routine by the third. Getting one project live now removes the fear before you need to deploy Elliot itself in Month 6.
_raw.missionDebrief: You now have a professional GitHub presence and, ideally, a live deployment. Next week you learn how apps fetch data - the bridge to React and to Elliot's backend.
_raw.commanderNotes: Your GitHub history is a public professional record from now on. Treat every commit message like a stranger will read it - because in a job search, one will.
_raw.nextMissionTeaser: Next week: fetch, JSON, and async thinking - how an app requests data and handles the wait, the foundation for every dynamic interface and every Elliot API call.

The error I got is: {errorMessage}. I have tried: {attempts}. Please help me debug this without giving me the full answer immediately.
practicalMissions.background: This drill isolates the fetch-then-render round trip and the async/await mechanics that make it readable.
hints: Console.log the parsed data before trying to render it, to confirm the fetch worked.
Deliberately misspell the path once to see exactly what a failed fetch looks like.
commonMistakes: Rendering before the data arrives because the fetch wasn't awaited.
debuggingChecklist: Confirm the function is async and both fetch and .json() are awaited.
Confirm the JSON path resolves (check Network tab).
thinkingPrompts: What does your code have at the moment right after `fetch(...)` but before `await`?
practicalMissions.stretchChallenge: Add a deliberate delay and confirm your loading message appears during it.
practicalMissions.realWorldApplications: Fetch-and-render is the core loop of every data-driven screen on the web.
practicalMissions.approachOutline: Create the JSON file first and confirm it is valid before any JavaScript touches it. Then fetch it inside an async function, await the response, and render the result. Log the parsed data before rendering — that single step separates "the request failed" from "the request worked and my rendering is wrong," which otherwise look identical on a blank page.
practicalMissions.scopeNote: This is the first mission where data arrives asynchronously. Code after a fetch does not run in the order it is written unless you await it, which is a different execution model from every mission so far.
practicalMissions.scopePromptTemplate:
I am on Week 10, Mission "Fetch + JSON Warm-Up Drill" of my JavaScript bootcamp.

What the mission asks for:
- Create resources.json.
- Use fetch to load JSON.
- Render resources as cards.

The concepts this mission is meant to exercise are: JSON as a data format, The fetch API, async / await, Rendering fetched data to the page.

Intended approach:
Create the JSON file first and confirm it is valid before any JavaScript touches it. Then fetch it inside an async function, await the response, and render the result. Log the parsed data before rendering — that single step separates "the request failed" from "the request worked and my rendering is wrong," which otherwise look identical on a blank page.

Important scope note: This is the first mission where data arrives asynchronously. Code after a fetch does not run in the order it is written unless you await it, which is a different execution model from every mission so far.

The error I got is: {errorMessage}. I have tried: {attempts}. Please help me debug this without giving me the full answer immediately.
practicalMissions.background: The Resource Fetch Board is a real data-driven interface - the pattern behind every list, feed, and dashboard Elliot will ever show.
hints: Render a loading message first, then replace it when data arrives - never show a blank screen during the wait.
Break the JSON path on purpose to build and test your error state, then restore it.
commonMistakes: Handling only the success path and leaving the screen blank or frozen on error.
Not checking response.ok, so a 404 silently renders nothing.
debuggingChecklist: Does a loading state show before data?
Does a forced error show a helpful message, not a blank page?
Does filtering (if added) work without breaking the render?
thinkingPrompts: What are the three states this board can be in (loading, error, loaded) and did you design all three?
practicalMissions.stretchChallenge: Add type filtering and a retry button that re-fetches after an error.
practicalMissions.realWorldApplications: Loading/error/empty state handling is exactly what production code reviewers look for.
practicalMissions.commanderNotes: Design for all three states - loading, error, loaded - not just success. That discipline is what makes this feel like a product, not a demo.
practicalMissions.approachOutline: Extend the warm-up with the two states a real interface needs beyond success: something shown while the request is in flight, and something shown when it fails. Test the failure path by deliberately breaking the path — a blank page with no message is the failure mode this mission exists to prevent.
practicalMissions.scopeNote: This continues the warm-up drill's board rather than starting a new one.

practicalMissions.background: Breaking the fetch path and recovering builds fluency with the most common async failure mode.
hints: A failed fetch shows in the Network tab in red - learn to read it there, not just in the console.
Document the exact failure and recovery in the README.
commonMistakes: Assuming a silent blank page means 'no data' when it actually means an unhandled fetch error.
debuggingChecklist: Run all test cases.
Confirm the error state renders and then recovers after the fix.
thinkingPrompts: How would you tell the difference between 'the data is empty' and 'the fetch failed'?
practicalMissions.stretchChallenge: Add a Commander Mode improvement such as caching the last successful data in localStorage.
practicalMissions.realWorldApplications: Distinguishing empty-vs-failed is a real UX decision products get wrong constantly.
practicalMissions.approachOutline: Run every test case, then misspell the data path so you can see how a failed fetch presents in both the console and the network panel, and repair it. Knowing which of those two surfaces shows the real cause is the transferable skill.
practicalMissions.scopeNote: This mission verifies and documents the week's work rather than adding features.

_raw.briefing: Study, practice, prove, and reflect on Fetch, JSON, and Async Thinking.
_raw.elliotConnection: Elliot will need reusable interface pieces: chat bubbles, project cards, notes, settings, resource cards. React teaches that structure.
concepts: Rendering fetched data to the DOM
_raw.scenario: Real products don't hard-code their data - they fetch it. This week Elliot learns to request JSON, wait for it without freezing, and render it as cards, handling the loading and error states that separate a real interface from a demo. This is the bridge between your front-end and Elliot's future backend.
learningObjectives: Read and reason about JSON data structures
Request data with fetch and handle the Promise with async/await
Show a loading state while data is in flight
Handle and display fetch errors gracefully
Render an array of fetched data as UI cards
_raw.expectedOutcome: A Resource Fetch Board that loads resources from a JSON file with fetch, shows a loading message, renders cards, handles errors, and optionally filters by type.
stretchGoals: Fetch from a real public API instead of a local JSON file.
Add a retry button that re-runs the fetch after an error.
hints: `await` only works inside an `async` function - marking the wrong function is the most common first error.
A fetch that 404s does NOT throw by default - you must check `response.ok` yourself.
commonMistakes: Expecting fetch to throw on a 404 - it resolves; you have to check response.ok manually.
Forgetting to `await` the fetch (or the `.json()`), so you get a Promise instead of data.
Never showing a loading state, so a slow fetch looks like a broken page.
debugChecklist: Is the function marked `async` where you use `await`?
Did you `await` both the fetch and the `.json()`?
Are you checking `response.ok` for non-200 responses?
Is the JSON path correct relative to the page?
Does the DevTools Network tab show the request and its status?
thinkingPrompts: Why doesn't JavaScript just freeze and wait for the data instead of using Promises?
What should the user see during the moment between requesting data and receiving it?
recallPrompts: What keyword must a function have to use `await` inside it?
Does fetch throw an error on a 404? What must you check instead?
_raw.missionReview: You made an interface that depends on data arriving over time - and handled the waiting and the failing. That's the exact skill every screen in Elliot's future backend-connected app needs.
_raw.progressNotes: Async thinking is a real conceptual step up. If loading and error states now feel like a requirement rather than an afterthought, you're thinking like a product engineer.
_raw.missionDebrief: You can now fetch and render data with proper loading/error handling. Next week React gives you a cleaner way to structure the interfaces that display it.
_raw.commanderNotes: The habit of always handling loading AND error states - not just the happy path - is what separates junior demos from shippable products. Build it now.
_raw.nextMissionTeaser: Next week: React components and props. The cards you rendered by hand this week become reusable, composable building blocks.

_raw.elliotConnection: A working Elliot interface must accept messages, save tasks, mark notes, and update progress. React state makes that possible.
_raw.scenario: The cards you rendered by hand in Month 2 become reusable building blocks this week. hints: Every component must be exported and imported to be used - a forgotten export is the most common first error.
JSX uses `className`, not `class`, and every list-rendered element needs a unique `key`.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to export a component (or import it), causing a confusing 'element type is invalid' error.
Using `class` instead of `className` in JSX.
Rendering a list without a `key` prop, triggering a warning and subtle bugs.
debugChecklist: Is the component exported from its file and imported where used?
Are you using `className` not `class`?
Does every list item have a unique `key`?
Do the prop names match between where you pass and where you read them?

thinkingPrompts: How is a React component just a function that returns UI, given props as arguments?

recallPrompts: What must you do to a component before another file can use it?

_raw.commanderNotes: Props flow one way - down, from parent to child. Holding that single rule in mind prevents most early React confusion.

practicalMissions.background: This drill isolates the immutability rule by having you break it once, on purpose, and feel why it matters.
hints: Try `tasks.push(...)` once, watch the UI fail to update, then fix it with `setTasks([...tasks, newTask])`.
A controlled input needs both value={state} and onChange={updateState}.
commonMistakes: Mutating the array and concluding 'state is broken' rather than 'I mutated instead of replaced'.
debuggingChecklist: Confirm every update creates a new array.
Confirm the input is fully controlled.
thinkingPrompts: Why can't React tell that a mutated array changed?
practicalMissions.stretchChallenge: Add a completed-toggle that flips one task's status immutably.
practicalMissions.realWorldApplications: Immutable updates are enforced across the entire React ecosystem (and Redux, and more).
practicalMissions.approachOutline: Hold the list in state, bind the input so its value comes from state and its changes write back to state, then add items by producing a new array rather than pushing into the existing one. React re-renders when it is handed a new value; modifying the old array in place changes the data without telling React anything happened, which looks like a broken interface rather than a state bug.
practicalMissions.scopeNote: Week 11's components only displayed data passed down to them. This week components own data that changes over time, which is what makes the interface interactive rather than static.
practicalMissions.scopePromptTemplate:
I am on Week 12, Mission "React State Warm-Up Drill" of my JavaScript bootcamp.

What the mission asks for:
- Add tasks through a form.
- Store tasks in useState.
- Mark tasks complete.

The concepts this mission is meant to exercise are: React state with useState, Controlled form inputs, Immutable state updates, Rendering a list from state.

Intended approach:
Hold the list in state, bind the input so its value comes from state and its changes write back to state, then add items by producing a new array rather than pushing into the existing one. React re-renders when it is handed a new value; modifying the old array in place changes the data without telling React anything happened, which looks like a broken interface rather than a state bug.

Important scope note: Week 11's components only displayed data passed down to them. This week components own data that changes over time, which is what makes the interface interactive rather than static.

hints: Reuse the immutable add/toggle/delete patterns consistently - one mental model for all three actions.

practicalMissions.commanderNotes: Build this cleanly - you'll effectively reuse its shape for Elliot's notes and task screens. Derive the count from state; never track it separately.
practicalMissions.approachOutline: Extend the warm-up with completion toggling, deletion, a count, and rejection of empty input. Derive the count from the list rather than storing it separately — two pieces of state describing the same fact will eventually disagree. Every update should produce a new array rather than modifying the current one.
