_raw.briefing: Study, practice, prove, and reflect on React State, Forms, and Lists.
_raw.elliotConnection: Elliot must load knowledge, remember notes, and recover after refresh. Effects and persistence make React apps feel alive.
_raw.scenario: Props display data; state remembers and changes it. This week Elliot's components come alive: a task console where users add, complete, and delete tasks, with the UI updating from state. This is the interactive core every Elliot screen - chat, notes, tasks - is built on.
learningObjectives: Add and update component state with useState
Build controlled inputs bound to state
Update arrays in state immutably (new array, not mutation)
Render, toggle, and delete list items
Derive a value (task count) from state
_raw.expectedOutcome: The React Task Console: add tasks via a controlled form, store them in state, mark complete, delete, show a live count, and validate empty input.
stretchGoals: Add all/active/completed filters.
Persist tasks to localStorage so they survive a refresh.
hints: Never mutate state directly - build a new array/object and pass it to the setter, or React won't re-render.
A controlled input's value comes from state and updates state on change - both directions must be wired.
commonMistakes: Mutating state directly (e.g., `tasks.push(...)`) instead of setting a new array, so the UI doesn't update.
Building an input whose value is set but whose onChange doesn't update state (or vice versa).
Forgetting a stable key on list items, causing incorrect re-renders when items change.
debugChecklist: Are you creating a NEW array/object for every state update, not mutating?
Is the input both reading from state (value) and writing to it (onChange)?
Does each task have a stable unique key?
Is the count derived from state, not tracked separately?
Does the console show any 'update during render' or key warnings?
thinkingPrompts: Why does React require a new array instead of letting you push to the existing one?
How is this task console structurally identical to Elliot's future notes and chat screens?
recallPrompts: What does useState return, and how do you update it?
Why must state updates be immutable?

months.description: Month 3 professionalizes how you build. It opens with GitHub discipline and deployment - turning private practice into public, shareable proof - then introduces fetch and asynchronous thinking (how apps talk to data), and finally React: the component-based library behind most modern product interfaces. By the end, everything you built by hand in Month 2 you can now build as reusable, stateful React components.
learningOutcome: Maintain a clean, documented GitHub repository and deploy a live app
Load and render external data asynchronously with fetch and JSON
Build reusable UI from React components and props
Manage interactive state with useState and render dynamic lists
Handle loading, error, and empty states like a professional
months.milestoneDescription: By the end of Month 3 you will have shipped the React Task Console: a component-based app where users add, complete, and delete tasks with live state - the reusable interface foundation Elliot's screens are built from.
months.motivation: React is the single most in-demand front-end skill in the JavaScript job market, and it powers both Elliot's web app and (via React Native) its mobile app. Learning it on top of hand-built DOM work means you understand not just how to use it, but why it exists.
months.recommendedPreparation: Be comfortable with Month 2's DOM manipulation and events - React automates exactly that work, so knowing the manual version makes React's model intuitive rather than magical.
months.careerInsight: React fundamentals - components, props, state, keys, the rules of hooks - are the core of virtually every front-end technical interview. This month is your most directly employable skill set so far.

_raw.briefing: Study, practice, prove, and reflect on Node.js and Express First Backend.

_raw.scenario: Elliot needs a brain behind the interface. This week you build its first backend: a Node/Express server with health and profile endpoints that return JSON. This is the beginning of the server layer that will eventually store Elliot's notes, tasks, knowledge, and chat.
learningObjectives: Initialize an npm project and install Express
Create an Express server that listens on a port
Define GET routes that return JSON
Serve data from a JSON file
Explain the request/response cycle end to end
_raw.expectedOutcome: An Elliot Profile API: an Express server with GET /health and GET /profile returning JSON from a data file, runnable via an npm script.
stretchGoals: Add a GET /projects endpoint returning an array from a JSON file.
Add a simple request logger that prints each incoming request's method and path.
hints: `node server.js` starts the server; it keeps running until you stop it - a stopped server is why endpoints suddenly 'fail'.
Express sends JSON with `res.json(data)` - it sets the right headers for you.
commonMistakes: Testing an endpoint while the server isn't running and concluding the code is broken.
Forgetting to actually call `app.listen(port)`, so the server never starts.
Editing server code but not restarting the server, so old behavior persists.
debugChecklist: Is the server actually running (did app.listen fire, is the port free)?
Did you restart the server after editing it?
Is the route path spelled exactly as you're requesting?
Does the JSON file exist at the path server.js reads?
Does the terminal show the request arriving or an error?
thinkingPrompts: What happens, step by step, between your browser requesting /profile and receiving JSON?
Why must a server keep running, unlike a script that finishes and exits?
recallPrompts: What Express method sends a JSON response?
Why does a stopped server make every endpoint fail?
_raw.missionReview: You built a server that answers requests. Elliot now has the beginnings of a backend - the layer that will hold everything it remembers.
_raw.progressNotes: The request/response cycle is the mental model behind all backend work. If you can trace a request from browser to server to JSON and back, the rest of Month 4 builds smoothly.
_raw.missionDebrief: Elliot has a backend that serves data. Next week it learns to change data too, with full CRUD.
_raw.commanderNotes: 'It failed' at the backend usually means 'the server isn't running' or 'I didn't restart it.' Check those two first, every time.
_raw.nextMissionTeaser: Next week: REST APIs and CRUD. Elliot's backend learns to create, read, update, and delete - the backbone of usable data.

Verify each route before writing the next.

_raw.briefing: Study, practice, prove, and reflect on REST APIs and CRUD.
_raw.elliotConnection: Elliot needs a brain behind the interface. This week starts the backend layer.
_raw.scenario: A backend that only reads is half a backend. This week Elliot's API learns full CRUD: create, read, update, and delete tasks, persisted to a JSON file. CRUD is the backbone of every usable data feature Elliot will have - notes, tasks, knowledge, all of it.
learningObjectives: Map CRUD operations to HTTP methods
Build GET/POST/PATCH/DELETE routes for a resource
Read a route parameter like :id
Parse JSON request bodies
Persist changes to a JSON file
_raw.expectedOutcome: An Elliot Tasks API with GET all, POST new, PATCH complete, and DELETE routes, file-based persistence, and validation that rejects empty tasks.
stretchGoals: Add input validation that returns a 400 with a clear message for bad requests.
Add a GET /tasks/:id route returning a single task or 404.
hints: Express needs `express.json()` middleware to read POST/PATCH bodies - without it, req.body is undefined.
Match the HTTP method to the intent: GET reads, POST creates, PATCH updates, DELETE removes.
commonMistakes: Forgetting express.json() middleware, so req.body is undefined on POST.
Using GET for actions that change data instead of POST/PATCH/DELETE.
Reading/writing the JSON file incorrectly so changes don't persist between requests.
debugChecklist: Is express.json() middleware registered before the routes?
Does each route use the correct HTTP method for its action?
Is :id parsed and matched correctly?
Are file writes actually saving (re-read to confirm)?
Do bad requests return a clear error, not a crash?
thinkingPrompts: Why does REST map different actions to different HTTP methods instead of one endpoint doing everything?
How is this tasks API the same shape as the notes API Elliot will also need?
recallPrompts: Which HTTP methods map to create, read, update, delete?
What middleware lets Express read a JSON request body?
_raw.missionReview: You built a full CRUD API with persistence. This is the single most reused backend pattern in the industry and the core of everything Elliot stores.
_raw.progressNotes: CRUD is the backbone skill of Month 4. If create/read/update/delete all persist correctly, you can build the data layer of almost any product.
_raw.missionDebrief: Elliot's backend can now manage data fully. Next week you connect it to the React front-end for a complete round trip.
_raw.commanderNotes: Match methods to intent honestly - GET never changes data. That discipline is what makes an API RESTful and predictable.
_raw.nextMissionTeaser: Next week: connect React to Express. The front-end and back-end finally talk, and Elliot becomes truly full-stack.

practicalMissions.background: This drill isolates the two-process setup and the first successful cross-origin fetch.
hints: Start the server, confirm its endpoint in the browser, THEN start the client and fetch it.
If the fetch is blocked, read the console - a CORS message is unmistakable.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to start the server before the client tries to fetch it.
debuggingChecklist: Confirm both processes run.
Confirm the client renders fetched tasks.
thinkingPrompts: What are the two processes that must both be alive for this to work, and how do you confirm each?
practicalMissions.stretchChallenge: Add a POST from a React form and confirm the new task appears after refetch.
practicalMissions.realWorldApplications: Running client and server together is the daily reality of full-stack development.
practicalMissions.approachOutline: Run both processes at once, on different ports, and confirm the API responds directly in the browser before asking React to call it — that isolates a backend problem from a frontend one. Then fetch on the client and render the result. A request blocked by cross-origin policy fails in a recognisably different way from one that simply 404s, and telling those apart is the core skill of this week.
practicalMissions.scopeNote: This is the first mission running two processes simultaneously. Until now each mission was either frontend or backend; here they must both be running and able to reach each other.
practicalMissions.scopePromptTemplate:
I am on Week 16, Mission "React + Express Integration Warm-Up Drill" of my JavaScript bootcamp.

What the mission asks for:
- Fetch tasks from backend.
- Add tasks from React form.
- Delete tasks from UI.

The concepts this mission is meant to exercise are: Running client and server together, Cross-origin requests and CORS, Fetching backend data from React, Rendering server data in a component.

Intended approach:
Run both processes at once, on different ports, and confirm the API responds directly in the browser before asking React to call it — that isolates a backend problem from a frontend one. Then fetch on the client and render the result. A request blocked by cross-origin policy fails in a recognisably different way from one that simply 404s, and telling those apart is the core skill of this week.

practicalMissions.realWorldApplications: A connected CRUD client is the archetype of virtually every SaaS product's core loop.

debuggingChecklist: Run test cases.

thinkingPrompts: How would you quickly tell a CORS block apart from a wrong-URL failure in the Network tab?

practicalMissions.approachOutline: Run every test case, then point the client at the wrong port so you can trace a failed request through the browser's network panel, and repair it. Reading the network panel rather than guessing is the habit this drill installs.

_raw.briefing: Study, practice, prove, and reflect on Connecting React to Express.
_raw.elliotConnection: Elliot must create, read, update, and delete notes/tasks. CRUD is the backbone of usable assistant data.
concepts: Loading and error states across the stack
_raw.scenario: This is the week the two halves meet. Elliot's React client fetches, adds, and deletes tasks through the Express API - a complete full-stack round trip. Handling CORS, loading, errors, and a server-offline state is what makes it a real application rather than two disconnected demos.
learningObjectives: Run a React client and Express server simultaneously
Fetch backend data into React and render it
POST and DELETE from the UI and update state
Configure CORS for cross-origin requests
Handle loading, error, and server-offline states
_raw.expectedOutcome: The Elliot Web Client + API: a React app that reads and writes tasks through the Express backend, with loading/error states and a clear message when the server is offline.
stretchGoals: Add optimistic UI updates that revert if the request fails.
Extract the fetch logic into a small reusable API helper module.
hints: A CORS error in the console means the browser blocked a cross-origin request - enable CORS on the Express side.
Run the server and the client in two separate terminals; both must be up for the app to work.
commonMistakes: Seeing a CORS error and editing the front-end when the fix belongs on the server (enable CORS).
Only running one of the two processes and wondering why requests fail.
Not handling the server-offline case, so the UI hangs or shows a cryptic error.
debugChecklist: Are both the client and server running (two terminals)?
Is CORS enabled on the server for the client's origin?
Does the Network tab show the request, its status, and any CORS block?
Does the UI update after a successful POST/DELETE?
Is there a clear message when the server is down?
thinkingPrompts: Why does the browser block cross-origin requests by default, and why is CORS the intended fix rather than a hack?
Which parts of Elliot's data flow are now identical to how the final product will work?
recallPrompts: What does a CORS error actually indicate?
Why must both the client and server processes be running?
_raw.missionReview: You connected a real front-end to a real back-end with full data flow and honest error handling. Elliot is now a genuine full-stack application - the Month 4 boss achievement.
_raw.progressNotes: Full-stack connection is where many learners feel it 'all come together.' If tasks flow from the UI to the file and back, you've built the core of a real product.
_raw.missionDebrief: Month 4 complete: Elliot is full-stack - a React client talking to an Express API with persistence. Month 5 makes it reliable, installable, and mobile.
_raw.commanderNotes: CORS errors are a server-side fix, not a front-end one. Remembering that single fact will save you hours across the rest of the bootcamp.
_raw.nextMissionTeaser: Month 5: reliability, validation, PWA installability, a real mobile audit of TheScoreboard, and your first React Native app on your Samsung A70.

months.description: Month 4 gives Elliot a brain behind its face. You start by structuring a multi-page React portfolio with routing, then build your first real backend with Node.js and Express, design a REST API with full CRUD, and finally connect the React front-end to the Express back-end so data flows both ways. By the end, Elliot is a genuine full-stack application: a UI talking to a server that stores and serves data.
learningOutcome: Build a multi-page React app with client-side routing and shared layout
Create a Node.js/Express server that returns JSON
Design a REST API with GET/POST/PATCH/DELETE and file-based persistence
Connect a React front-end to an Express back-end across origins (CORS)
Handle loading, error, and offline states across the full stack
months.milestoneDescription: By the end of Month 4 you will have a connected full-stack Elliot: a React web client that reads and writes tasks through an Express REST API with file-based storage - the backbone of the final product.
months.motivation: Full-stack ability - owning both the interface and the server - is what lets one person build a whole product. This month is where Elliot stops being a front-end demo and becomes a real application with a data layer.
months.recommendedPreparation: Be solid on Month 3's React state and fetch/async - the front-end half of full-stack builds directly on both, and Month 1's objects/JSON become your API payloads.
months.careerInsight: 'Can you build a CRUD API and wire a front-end to it?' is the single most common practical test in junior full-stack interviews and take-homes. This month is that exact skill, end to end.

_raw.elliotConnection: Assistants must not silently fail. Elliot needs predictable responses, helpful errors, and safer boundaries.
_raw.scenario: Assistants must not silently fail. This week Elliot's settings panel learns to validate input, show clear errors, and recover gracefully - the reliability layer that makes a product trustworthy instead of fragile.
learningObjectives: Build a settings form with controlled inputs
Validate required fields before saving
Display clear error messages with an ErrorBanner
Persist valid settings and confirm they survive reload
Handle corrupted or invalid stored data without crashing
_raw.expectedOutcome: An Elliot Settings and Validation Panel that rejects empty name/weekly-hours input with a clear error, saves valid settings to localStorage, and recovers gracefully from invalid stored JSON.
stretchGoals: Add field-specific error messages instead of one generic banner.
Add a 'reset to defaults' action that clears corrupted settings safely.
hints: Validate before you save, not after - catching bad input early prevents it from ever reaching storage.
Wrap JSON.parse of stored data in try...catch; a corrupted string will otherwise crash the app on load.
commonMistakes: Saving invalid data first and only checking it later, letting bad state slip through.
Letting a JSON.parse failure throw uncaught and crash the whole app on load.
Showing a generic 'error' message that doesn't tell the user what to actually fix.
debugChecklist: Does validation run before any save?
Is JSON.parse wrapped in try...catch with a fallback?
Does the error message say specifically what's wrong?
Does reloading with valid settings show them correctly?
Does reloading with corrupted localStorage recover instead of crashing?
thinkingPrompts: Why should a settings panel never trust its own previously-saved data blindly?
How is this validation pattern the same one Elliot's backend will need for every API request?
recallPrompts: What does try...catch let you do that a plain function call doesn't?
Why validate before saving rather than after?

_raw.progressNotes: Validation and error handling are unglamorous compared to features, but they are what separates a demo from something you'd trust with real use. This is professional maturity, not busywork.
_raw.missionDebrief: Elliot's settings are now trustworthy. Next week the whole portfolio becomes installable as a Progressive Web App.

The error I got is: {errorMessage}. I have tried: {attempts}. Please help me debug this without giving me the full answer immediately.
practicalMissions.background: This drill isolates the manifest-plus-link mechanic that makes installability possible at all.
hints: Create the manifest, link it, then use DevTools 'Application' > 'Manifest' to confirm the browser parsed it.
Start with one icon size to prove the pipeline before adding more.
commonMistakes: Creating a manifest that's never actually linked from the HTML.
debuggingChecklist: Confirm the manifest link is in the HTML head.
Confirm DevTools shows the manifest parsed without errors.
thinkingPrompts: How would you verify, without guessing, that the browser actually found your manifest?
practicalMissions.stretchChallenge: Add a theme_color that changes the browser chrome color on mobile.
practicalMissions.realWorldApplications: Every installable web app - from Twitter to Starbucks - starts with exactly this manifest setup.
futureConcepts: Full PWA upgrade (this week's main build)
practicalMissions.approachOutline: Write the manifest, then link it from the page and confirm the browser actually parsed it using the developer tools application panel. A manifest that exists but is never linked, or is linked at a path that does not resolve, fails without any error at all — verifying it was read is the only reliable check.
practicalMissions.scopeNote: This week is configuration rather than programming: the work is metadata, icons, and paths, and the failures are silent rather than thrown.
practicalMissions.scopePromptTemplate:
I am on Week 18, Mission "PWA Warm-Up Drill" of my JavaScript bootcamp.

What the mission asks for:
- Add app manifest.
- Add icons/placeholders.
- Improve mobile layout.

The concepts this mission is meant to exercise are: Web app manifest, App icons and theme colour, Linking a manifest to a page, Mobile viewport behaviour.

Intended approach:
Write the manifest, then link it from the page and confirm the browser actually parsed it using the developer tools application panel. A manifest that exists but is never linked, or is linked at a path that does not resolve, fails without any error at all — verifying it was read is the only reliable check.

Important scope note: This week is configuration rather than programming: the work is metadata, icons, and paths, and the failures are silent rather than thrown.

The error I got is: {errorMessage}. I have tried: {attempts}. Please help me debug this without giving me the full answer immediately.
practicalMissions.background: The Portfolio PWA Upgrade is Elliot's cheapest, fastest path to a phone's home screen - before any native app exists.
hints: Provide at least 192x192 and 512x512 icons - installability checks specifically look for these.
Document the exact install steps (browser menu > 'Add to Home Screen') so a real user could follow them.
commonMistakes: Providing only one icon size and having installability silently fail.
Polishing desktop styling but never testing the real mobile viewport.
debuggingChecklist: Do both required icon sizes exist and resolve?
Does the app show an install prompt or pass a basic Lighthouse installability check?
Is mobile layout genuinely usable, not just 'not broken'?
thinkingPrompts: What's the actual difference in effort between this PWA upgrade and building a full native app - and when is each worth it?
practicalMissions.stretchChallenge: Add a minimal service worker caching the app shell for basic offline load.
practicalMissions.realWorldApplications: PWAs are a real, common product strategy for reaching mobile users before investing in native apps.
practicalMissions.commanderNotes: This is the cheapest mobile reach you'll ever get. Treat the manifest and icons with real care - the payoff is a phone home-screen icon by end of week.
practicalMissions.approachOutline: Extend the warm-up manifest with the icon sizes installability actually requires, improve the layout at phone width, and write install instructions a real person could follow. Verify against an installability check rather than assuming the manifest alone is sufficient, and confirm every icon path resolves.

practicalMissions.helpPromptTemplate: I am on Week {weekNumber}, Mission {missionNumber} of the XcelerateAI Bootcamp. I am trying to build {missionTitle}. I created these files: {filesCreated}. The error I got is: {errorMessage}. I have tried: {attempts}. Please help me debug this without giving me the full answer immediately.
practicalMissions.background: Breaking the manifest path on purpose and fixing it builds precise intuition for PWA's silent failure modes.
hints: A wrong manifest path fails silently - no error, just no install prompt. Confirm via DevTools, not guessing.
Document the broken path and the fix.
commonMistakes: Assuming 'no install prompt' means the browser doesn't support PWAs, when it's actually a broken manifest link.
debuggingChecklist: Run test cases.
Confirm DevTools shows a valid, error-free manifest after the fix.
thinkingPrompts: Why does a broken manifest path fail silently instead of showing an error?
practicalMissions.stretchChallenge: Add a Commander Mode improvement such as a custom splash screen color.
practicalMissions.realWorldApplications: Silent PWA installability failures are a common, hard-to-notice production bug.
practicalMissions.approachOutline: Run every test case, then point the manifest link at a path that does not exist so you can observe that nothing visibly breaks, and repair it. Learning that this failure is silent is the entire point of the drill.
practicalMissions.scopeNote: This mission verifies and documents the week's work rather than adding features.
practicalMissions.scopePromptTemplate:
I am on Week 18, Mission "Week 18 Debug, Upgrade, and Proof" of my JavaScript bootcamp.

What the mission asks for:
- Run all test cases.
- Create one intentional bug and fix it.
- Add a Commander Mode improvement if time allows.
- Write proof in README.

The concepts this mission is meant to exercise are: Systematic verification against test cases, Diagnosing a silent manifest failure, Documenting a fix.

Intended approach:
Run every test case, then point the manifest link at a path that does not exist so you can observe that nothing visibly breaks, and repair it. Learning that this failure is silent is the entire point of the drill.

Important scope note: This mission verifies and documents the week's work rather than adding features.

_raw.scenario: Your portfolio and TheScoreboard can reach phones before a full native app exists. This week you make the portfolio installable: a manifest, icons, and mobile polish that let it live on a phone's home screen like a real app - Elliot's cheapest path to mobile reach.
learningObjectives: Create and link a web app manifest
Set an app name, theme color, and icons

hints: The manifest must be linked with `<link rel="manifest" href="/manifest.json">` in the HTML head - a missing link means no install prompt.
Icons need multiple sizes (192x192, 512x512 minimum) for installability checks to pass.

Using a single icon size, failing installability requirements.
Never actually testing installability, assuming the manifest alone is enough.
debugChecklist: Is the manifest linked in the HTML head?
Do the icon paths in the manifest actually resolve?
Are at least two icon sizes provided?
Does the manifest's start_url and scope make sense?
Have you tested at real mobile viewport width?

This is a different, valuable skill from building fresh - most professional work is improving something that already exists.
learningObjectives: Audit a real product's mobile experience methodically
Understand and query the WordPress REST API
Design a mobile-first user flow
Build a small fetch prototype against a live external API
Document findings and a plan for someone else to act on

stretchGoals: Render fetched WordPress posts as styled cards in the prototype.

hints: WordPress REST endpoints typically live under `/wp-json/wp/v2/posts` - confirm the exact base URL for the real site first.

commonMistakes: Writing vague audit notes ('mobile is bad') instead of specific, actionable observations.

Designing an ideal mobile flow with no connection to what the REST API can actually provide.

practicalMissions.helpPromptTemplate: I am on Week {weekNumber}, Mission {missionNumber} of the XcelerateAI Bootcamp. I am trying to build {missionTitle}. I created these files: {filesCreated}. The error I got is: {errorMessage}. I have tried: {attempts}. Please help me debug this without giving me the full answer immediately.
practicalMissions.background: This drill isolates the Expo setup ritual and the QR-code device connection before the full mobile shell.
hints: Confirm the Expo dev server starts cleanly in the terminal before scanning the QR code.
If the connection fails, check Wi-Fi network match first - it's the most common cause.
commonMistakes: Phone on cellular data or a different Wi-Fi network than the laptop, so Expo Go can't find the dev server.
debuggingChecklist: Confirm phone and laptop share a Wi-Fi network.
Confirm the dev server terminal shows no errors.
thinkingPrompts: What has to be true on the network level for a QR code to actually connect your phone to your laptop's dev server?
practicalMissions.stretchChallenge: Edit App.js while the app is open on your phone and time how fast live reload reflects the change.
practicalMissions.realWorldApplications: Physical-device testing via Expo Go is the standard workflow for React Native development.
futureConcepts: Full mobile shell (this week's main build)
practicalMissions.approachOutline: Create the project, start the development server, and connect the phone before writing any interface code — the connection is the part most likely to fail and the least related to your code. Once an edit appears live on the device, build screens from React Native's own components. There is no HTML here: text must sit inside a text component, and styling comes from style objects rather than CSS files.
practicalMissions.scopeNote: This is the first mission that leaves the browser entirely. The component model carries over from React, but the elements and the styling system do not — nothing you wrote for the web renders here unchanged.
practicalMissions.scopePromptTemplate:
I am on Week 20, Mission "React Native + Expo Warm-Up Drill" of my JavaScript bootcamp.

What the mission asks for:
- Create Expo app.
- Run on Samsung A70 using Expo Go.
- Create Home, Projects, Elliot placeholder screens.

The concepts this mission is meant to exercise are: Expo project setup, Running an app on a physical device, React Native core components, StyleSheet-based styling.

Intended approach:
Create the project, start the development server, and connect the phone before writing any interface code — the connection is the part most likely to fail and the least related to your code. Once an edit appears live on the device, build screens from React Native's own components. There is no HTML here: text must sit inside a text component, and styling comes from style objects rather than CSS files.

Important scope note: This is the first mission that leaves the browser entirely. The component model carries over from React, but the elements and the styling system do not — nothing you wrote for the web renders here unchanged.

practicalMissions.background: The Portfolio Mobile Shell is Elliot's first real native screen structure - the direct ancestor of its full mobile app in Month 6.
hints: Build one screen fully (structure, basic styling) before duplicating the pattern for the other two.
Keep styling simple this week - navigation and polish are Month 6's job.
commonMistakes: Trying to import web CSS or HTML patterns instead of using View/Text/StyleSheet.
Building all three screens' logic before confirming even one renders correctly on the device.
debuggingChecklist: Do all three screens render on the physical device?
Is all text wrapped in Text components?
Does the app reflect edits live without a full restart?
thinkingPrompts: When you add real navigation next week, what will need to change about how these three screens are structured?
practicalMissions.stretchChallenge: Add basic tab or stack navigation connecting the three screens.
practicalMissions.realWorldApplications: A running Expo app on a real device is the literal starting point of every React Native product, including Elliot.
practicalMissions.commanderNotes: This is Month 5's flagship mobile milestone. When it runs on your own A70, you've crossed into real mobile development - a significant, real achievement.
practicalMissions.approachOutline: Extend the warm-up into three screens with basic styling. Build one screen completely and confirm it renders on the device before duplicating the pattern — a layout problem repeated across three screens is three times the work to unpick.
practicalMissions.scopeNote: This continues the warm-up drill's Expo project rather than creating another.

practicalMissions.background: Disconnecting the phone or stopping the server and observing the failure, then correctly restarting, builds real mobile-dev operational intuition.
hints: A disconnected app on the phone shows a distinct error screen - learn to recognize and recover from it.
Document the exact disconnect/reconnect sequence in the README.
commonMistakes: Panicking and reinstalling everything instead of simply restarting the dev server and reconnecting.
debuggingChecklist: Run test cases.
Confirm the app reconnects cleanly after restart.
thinkingPrompts: What's the fastest, least destructive way to recover from a dropped Expo connection?
practicalMissions.stretchChallenge: Add a Commander Mode improvement such as a loading placeholder shown while the app connects.
practicalMissions.realWorldApplications: Connection drops between device and dev server are routine in real mobile development - fast recovery is a practical skill.
practicalMissions.approachOutline: Run every test case, then stop the development server or disconnect the device so you can see how that presents on the phone, and reconnect correctly. Dropped connections are routine in mobile development; recovering quickly without rebuilding anything is the skill.
practicalMissions.scopeNote: This mission verifies and documents the week's work rather than adding features.

_raw.scenario: Elliot must live on your phone. This week you leave the browser for the first time and build a real mobile app with React Native and Expo, running live on your Samsung A70 - no heavy emulator required. This is the skill Elliot's mobile client is built on for the rest of the bootcamp.
learningObjectives: Set up the Expo development environment

Run the app on a physical device via Expo Go
Understand View, Text, and Button as React Native's building blocks

_raw.expectedOutcome: A Portfolio Mobile Shell v1: an Expo app with Home, Projects, and Elliot placeholder screens, running live on your Samsung A70, styled with basic React Native styling.
stretchGoals: Add simple navigation between the three placeholder screens.
Style each screen with a distinct accent color matching your portfolio brand.
hints: React Native has no HTML tags - `View` replaces `div`, `Text` replaces `p`/`span`; text must always be inside a `<Text>` component.
If the QR code won't connect, confirm your phone and laptop are on the same Wi-Fi network first.
commonMistakes: Trying to render raw text outside a `<Text>` component, which React Native rejects.
Assuming CSS class names work the same way - React Native uses StyleSheet objects, not CSS files.
Phone and laptop on different networks, so Expo Go can never find the dev server.
debugChecklist: Is all visible text wrapped in a `<Text>` component?
Are styles defined via StyleSheet.create, not CSS?
Are the phone and laptop on the same Wi-Fi network?
Does editing App.js trigger a live reload on the phone?
Does the terminal show the Expo dev server running without errors?
thinkingPrompts: Why does React Native need its own components (View, Text) instead of reusing HTML tags?

recallPrompts: What component must all visible text be wrapped in?

You harden the front-end and back-end against bad input and errors, make the portfolio installable as a Progressive Web App, apply mobile-product thinking to a real existing system (TheScoreboard), and - the big shift - leave the browser entirely and run your first React Native app on your own phone with Expo. practicalMissions.background: This drill isolates navigation setup and a minimal storage read/write before the full Notes screen.
hints: Get two screens navigating back and forth before adding storage.
Await every storage call - treat it like a mini version of Month 3's fetch/async work.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to register a screen, causing a 'screen not found' navigation error.
debuggingChecklist: Confirm both screens are registered in the navigator.
Confirm storage reads are awaited.
thinkingPrompts: What's the minimum setup needed for two screens to navigate to each other?
practicalMissions.stretchChallenge: Pass a parameter from one screen to another via navigation.
practicalMissions.realWorldApplications: Multi-screen navigation with local storage is the skeleton of nearly every mobile app.
futureConcepts: Full mobile notes (this week's main build)
practicalMissions.approachOutline: Get two screens navigating between each other before adding storage — those are independent problems and much easier to debug apart. Device storage is asynchronous, unlike the browser storage used in Week 8, so reads and writes must be awaited; code that reads without awaiting receives a pending operation rather than the value. A screen that cannot be reached is usually unregistered rather than broken.
practicalMissions.scopeNote: Storage here behaves differently from Week 8's browser storage: it is asynchronous, so values are not available on the line after you ask for them.

practicalMissions.approachOutline: Extend the warm-up into a working notes screen with listing and deletion, persisted across launches. practicalMissions.background: This drill isolates the message array, keying, and controlled input before the full chat UI is built.
hints: Assign each sample message a unique id up front - don't rely on array position.
Render messages in order and confirm the list updates when you add one.
commonMistakes: Reusing the same id for two messages, causing a React key warning and rendering glitches.
debuggingChecklist: Confirm every message id is unique.
Confirm the input updates state as the user types.
thinkingPrompts: What real-world event would cause two messages to briefly have colliding ids if you're not careful?

practicalMissions.realWorldApplications: Correct list-keying is essential in every chat, feed, or comment interface.
futureConcepts: Full chat UI (this week's main build)
practicalMissions.approachOutline: Model a message as an object carrying its own identity, its sender, and its text, then render the list in order. Give each message a stable identifier of its own rather than relying on its position, because positions shift as messages are added. Get the list rendering from fixed sample data before wiring the input.
practicalMissions.scopeNote: This mission is built twice, once for web and once for mobile. Keep the message shape identical across both so a single backend can serve them later.

_raw.briefing: Study, practice, prove, and reflect on Chat Interface for Elliot.
_raw.elliotConnection: A real assistant product is not just screens. It connects to a backend that stores and serves knowledge, notes, tasks, and document data.
_raw.scenario: A real assistant product is not just screens - it talks back. This week Elliot gets a chat interface on both web and mobile: a message list, an input, a send action, and a mock assistant reply. This is the interaction pattern the whole product has been building toward.
learningObjectives: Model chat messages as an array of objects
Render user and assistant messages distinctly
Build a controlled input with a send action
Add a mock assistant response on send
Keep message lists correctly keyed and ordered
_raw.expectedOutcome: Elliot Chat UI v1: a chat window (web and mobile) that renders message history, accepts new input, sends it, shows a mock assistant reply, and auto-clears the input.
stretchGoals: Add a typing indicator shown briefly before the mock reply appears.
Style user and assistant bubbles with distinct colors and alignment.
hints: Give every message a stable unique id (not the array index) for its React key - array-index keys break when messages are added.
Auto-scroll to the newest message after each send so the conversation reads naturally.
commonMistakes: Using the array index as the key, causing subtle bugs when messages are added or reordered.
Not clearing the input after send, so users accidentally resend the same text.
Forgetting to distinguish user vs. assistant messages visually, making the conversation unreadable.
debugChecklist: Does every message have a stable unique id used as its key?
Does the input clear after sending?
Are user and assistant messages visually distinct?
Does the list auto-scroll or stay readable as it grows?
Does sending an empty message get rejected?
thinkingPrompts: Why is a stable message id better than the array index as a React key here?
What would change about this chat UI once it talks to a real backend instead of a mock reply?
recallPrompts: Why shouldn't you use array index as a list key for chat messages?
What should happen to the input field immediately after sending a message?
_raw.missionReview: Elliot finally feels like an assistant - a real conversational interface, even before the backend behind it is smart. The interaction shape is exactly right.
_raw.progressNotes: This is one of the most satisfying missions in the bootcamp because it 'feels like Elliot.' Notice how much of the hard work (state, lists, controlled inputs) was already learned in Month 3 - this week mostly applies it.
_raw.missionDebrief: Elliot can hold a conversation shape, even with mock replies. Next week the replies get real: knowledge, uploads, and basic understanding.
_raw.commanderNotes: This is the mission most learners screenshot first. It's the moment Elliot stops looking like an exercise and starts looking like a product.
_raw.nextMissionTeaser: Next week: knowledge and uploads. Elliot's replies stop being mocked and start coming from real data you give it.

practicalMissions.background: Feature freezing is a genuine professional skill - most shipped products succeed by cutting scope deliberately, not by finishing everything imagined.
hints: List every tempting feature, then move most of them to a written V2 section rather than deleting the ambition entirely.
Acceptance criteria should be testable facts ('chat sends and receives a message'), not vague aspirations ('chat works well').
commonMistakes: Writing acceptance criteria too vague to verify objectively.
debuggingChecklist: Is every acceptance criterion something you can check yes/no?
Is the V2 list honest and specific, not just 'more features'?
thinkingPrompts: What's the real cost of adding one more feature this week instead of polishing what exists?
practicalMissions.stretchChallenge: Rank your V2 list by expected value to prioritize what comes after graduation.
practicalMissions.realWorldApplications: Scope freezing under deadline pressure is one of the most valuable, transferable product skills in this bootcamp.
practicalMissions.approachOutline: This mission produces decisions, not code. List everything the product could do, then draw a line: what ships in this version, and what is explicitly deferred. Write acceptance criteria as statements that can be checked true or false, since criteria you cannot verify cannot tell you when to stop. Recording deferred features rather than deleting them is what makes the cut sustainable.
practicalMissions.scopeNote: The output of this mission is written scope and criteria rather than working software — it is the planning step the rest of the week depends on.

practicalMissions.background: Feature freezing is a genuine professional skill - most shipped products succeed by cutting scope deliberately, not by finishing everything imagined.
hints: List every tempting feature, then move most of them to a written V2 section rather than deleting the ambition entirely.
Acceptance criteria should be testable facts ('chat sends and receives a message'), not vague aspirations ('chat works well').
commonMistakes: Writing acceptance criteria too vague to verify objectively.
debuggingChecklist: Is every acceptance criterion something you can check yes/no?
Is the V2 list honest and specific, not just 'more features'?
thinkingPrompts: What's the real cost of adding one more feature this week instead of polishing what exists?
practicalMissions.stretchChallenge: Rank your V2 list by expected value to prioritize what comes after graduation.
practicalMissions.realWorldApplications: Scope freezing under deadline pressure is one of the most valuable, transferable product skills in this bootcamp.
practicalMissions.approachOutline: This mission produces decisions, not code. List everything the product could do, then draw a line: what ships in this version, and what is explicitly deferred. Write acceptance criteria as statements that can be checked true or false, since criteria you cannot verify cannot tell you when to stop. Recording deferred features rather than deleting them is what makes the cut sustainable.
practicalMissions.scopeNote: The output of this mission is written scope and criteria rather than working software — it is the planning step the rest of the week depends on.

practicalMissions.background: This is the web half of Elliot's graduation boss mission - proving chat, notes/tasks, and knowledge work together as one coherent product, not three disconnected demos.
hints: Connect the pieces in the order they depend on each other: backend up, then notes/tasks, then knowledge, then chat referencing both.
Test with the backend deliberately turned off - a clear error beats a frozen or broken UI.
commonMistakes: Testing each feature only in isolation and never as one connected user journey.
Leaving the offline/error path untested until a stranger hits it during the demo.
debuggingChecklist: Does chat work end to end?
Do notes/tasks save and persist through the real backend?
Does knowledge search return a real answer?
Is there a clear error state when the backend is off?
thinkingPrompts: If you demoed this live to a stranger right now, what's the first thing likely to go wrong?
practicalMissions.stretchChallenge: Add a guided first-run experience that briefly explains what Elliot can do.
practicalMissions.realWorldApplications: Full-system integration testing is exactly what separates 'features exist' from 'the product works.'
practicalMissions.commanderNotes: This is the web half of your final boss mission. Test the full user journey end to end, not each feature in isolation - that's where integration bugs hide.
practicalMissions.approachOutline: Bring up the layers in dependency order — backend first, then the client against it, then each feature in turn — verifying at each stage rather than connecting everything and testing once. Then walk the whole thing as a user would, in one continuous pass, because integration faults appear between features rather than inside them. Test with the backend deliberately stopped: a clear message there is the difference between a demo that degrades and one that appears broken.
practicalMissions.scopeNote: This mission connects work built across several months rather than adding new features. Everything it needs already exists in earlier missions.

Judge readability and touch targets on the actual phone — a layout that is fine on a laptop can be unusable in the hand.

practicalMissions.background: Deployment and demo craft turn a working codebase into something the outside world can actually evaluate - the final, essential step of shipping.
hints: Write the README for a stranger who has thirty seconds and no context - lead with what Elliot does, not how it's built.
A short, honest demo script (even without recording) is far better than an ambitious one you never finish.
commonMistakes: Writing a README that assumes deep familiarity with the bootcamp instead of explaining Elliot from zero.
Skipping screenshots or a demo entirely because 'the code speaks for itself' - it doesn't, to someone who won't run it.
debuggingChecklist: Could a stranger set up and run Elliot from your README alone?
Do screenshots/demo accurately reflect the current, real state of the product?
Is the V2 roadmap specific and credible, not vague?
Is the final commit pushed and the deployed link (if any) live?
thinkingPrompts: If someone asked to have someone (or an AI) follow your README cold, what's the first place they'd likely get stuck?
practicalMissions.stretchChallenge: Record an actual short demo video walking through Elliot's core features.
practicalMissions.realWorldApplications: A polished README, demo, and release notes are exactly what turns a project into a portfolio piece that gets you hired.
practicalMissions.commanderNotes: This is graduation. Read your own README as if you'd never seen the project before - fix whatever confuses you first. That's the real bar for done means done.
practicalMissions.approachOutline: Write the documentation for someone encountering the project cold: what it does before how it is built, and setup steps precise enough to follow literally. Then follow your own instructions from a clean starting point — the gap between what you wrote and what you actually did is where every unclear step hides. Capture evidence that reflects the real current state rather than the intended one.
practicalMissions.scopeNote: This final mission packages and communicates the work rather than changing it. Its audience is someone who has never seen the project.

_raw.briefing: Study, practice, prove, and reflect on Final Assembly: Elliot V1 Working Product.
_raw.elliotConnection: This is the graduation mission: a working assistant product, not a foundation. It should run on web/mobile, connect to backend, save notes/tasks, understand basic documents, and answer from your world.
_raw.scenario: This is the graduation mission: a working assistant product, not a foundation. You freeze scope, integrate web, mobile, backend, notes/tasks, knowledge, and chat into one coherent system, deploy it, and produce a demo a stranger could follow. Elliot V1 becomes real, not aspirational.
learningObjectives: Deliberately freeze V1 scope and defend what's postponed to V2
Integrate chat, notes/tasks, and knowledge into one cohesive web product
Integrate the same core features into the mobile app
Deploy and verify the product in something close to a real environment
Produce a README and demo that let a stranger understand and evaluate Elliot
_raw.expectedOutcome: Elliot V1 Working Product: a connected web and mobile assistant with chat, notes/tasks, and basic knowledge, deployed or demo-ready, with a complete README, demo script, and screenshots.
stretchGoals: Record an actual demo video instead of only a written script.
Write a genuine V2 roadmap reflecting what you'd build next with more time.
hints: Freeze scope in writing first - decide what's V1 and what's V2 before touching more code, or the deadline will decide for you badly.
Test the 'server offline' and 'first run' paths explicitly - these are what a stranger following your README will actually hit.
commonMistakes: Continuing to add features after the freeze instead of polishing and integrating what exists.
Testing only the happy path and skipping what happens when the backend is off or a screen is empty.
Writing a README for yourself (who already knows everything) instead of a stranger encountering the project cold.
debugChecklist: Is the scope genuinely frozen, with a written V2 list for anything tempting?
Does the web app work when the backend is intentionally stopped, with a clear message?
Does the mobile app run and connect on the physical device?
Does the README let a stranger set up and run the project from scratch?
Do screenshots and/or a demo video accurately represent the current, real product?
thinkingPrompts: What's the difference between a product that 'could do more' and one that 'does what it claims reliably'?
If you had to explain Elliot V1 to a stranger in 30 seconds, what would you say - and does your README say that?
recallPrompts: Why freeze scope before final integration, rather than after?
What are the two environments (web, mobile) V1 must demonstrably work in?
_raw.missionReview: You shipped a real, working, multi-layer product - not a collection of exercises, a system. Every one of the last 23 weeks is a load-bearing part of what you just integrated.
_raw.progressNotes: Integration weeks are humbling - things that worked in isolation reveal friction when connected. That friction is real engineering, and pushing through it is the actual graduation requirement.
_raw.missionDebrief: Elliot V1 is complete: web and mobile interfaces, a backend, notes/tasks memory, basic document understanding, and chat, deployed and documented. This is proof, not a promise.
_raw.commanderNotes: You are not building a perfect product this week - you are shipping an honest, working one. 'Done' beats 'perfect but unfinished.' Freeze scope, integrate, ship.
_raw.nextMissionTeaser: Beyond this bootcamp: TypeScript, a real database, deeper AI integration, app-store publishing, and everything else on your V2 list - now with a real, working V1 as the foundation to build from.

months.description: This is the assembly month. Every skill from the previous five months - JavaScript fundamentals, DOM and browser APIs, React, Node/Express, REST APIs, PWA, and React Native - gets connected into one working product. You build Elliot's mobile navigation and storage, its chat interface, its knowledge and document handling, and finally freeze scope, integrate everything across web and mobile, and ship a demoable, graduation-ready V1. This month is not about learning new frameworks; it is about proving everything you've learned works together.
learningOutcome: Build multi-screen React Native apps with navigation and local persistence
Build a chat-style interface shared conceptually across web and mobile
Handle file/text uploads and build a basic searchable knowledge feature
Freeze product scope deliberately and defend the decision
Integrate web, mobile, and backend into one coherent, demoable product
Deploy, document, and demo a complete full-stack product
months.milestoneDescription: By the end of Month 6 you will have shipped Elliot V1: a working assistant product running on web and mobile, connected to a backend, with notes/tasks memory, basic document understanding, and a public demo - your bootcamp capstone.
months.motivation: This is the month your six months of separate skills stop being separate. Elliot V1 is proof - to yourself and to anyone who reviews your portfolio - that you can take an ambiguous product idea from nothing to a working, demoable system entirely on your own.
months.recommendedPreparation: Have Month 4's full-stack connection and Month 5's Expo app both working and understood - this month connects and extends both rather than introducing new fundamentals.
months.careerInsight: A completed, demoable, multi-layer product like Elliot V1 is exactly what separates a portfolio of disconnected tutorials from a portfolio that gets interviews. 'I built and shipped a full-stack product across web, mobile, and backend' is a genuine, defensible claim after this month.

Appendix A - README Template
Use this template inside each mission folder or weekly folder.

# Mission Title ## Roadmap Week Week __ - ____________________ ## What I Built Write 3-5 lines explaining the mission. ## Files Created - index.html / App.jsx / server.js / etc. ## How To Run Write the exact command or browser steps. ## Features Completed - [ ] Feature 1 - [ ] Feature 2 - [ ] Feature 3 ## Test Results - Test 1: Pass/Fail - Test 2: Pass/Fail ## Bugs Faced Describe the bug and how you fixed it. ## Elliot Connection Explain how this mission helps build Elliot V1.
Appendix B - Ask Lemont Debug Prompt
Use this whenever you are blocked. Replace the blanks with your real mission details.
Appendix C - Final Elliot V1 Acceptance Standard
Elliot V1 is not complete because it looks nice. Elliot V1 is complete when it performs useful assistant behavior and has proof that it can be run, tested, and explained.
Web interface exists and is usable.
Mobile interface or mobile-tested version exists.
Chat interface works with user and assistant messages.
Notes or tasks can be saved.
Basic personal/project knowledge can be displayed or queried.
Backend API exists or local mock backend is clearly documented.
Basic text upload/paste understanding exists.
README explains how to run the project.
GitHub repository is organized.
Demo path is documented or recorded.
V2 features are clearly separated from V1 scope.

checkpoints.question: Can I install, verify, and use VS Code, Node, npm, Git, and GitHub without panic?
checkpoints.whyThisMatters: Every other checkpoint assumes your environment just works. This is the one that makes that assumption safe.
signsOfConfidence: You install a new tool without anxiety.
You read a terminal error and know where to look first.
You've broken and recovered your setup at least once.

checkpoints.question: Can I use variables, functions, arrays, objects, loops, JSON, and conditionals to model real project data?
checkpoints.whyThisMatters: Every framework and backend tool in this bootcamp is JavaScript underneath. Shaky fundamentals here resurface as confusion in every later month.
signsOfConfidence: You can model real data with arrays and objects without hesitation.
You can explain `==` vs `===` and type coercion with a concrete example.
You debug by reasoning, not by guessing and re-running.

checkpoints.question: Can I build pages that respond to clicks, forms, and saved local data?
checkpoints.whyThisMatters: React automates the DOM - it doesn't replace understanding it. This checkpoint is what makes React feel like a shortcut instead of magic.
signsOfConfidence: You can predict what a DOM change will do before running it.
You understand why events, not polling, drive interactivity.
localStorage's string-only nature no longer surprises you.

checkpoints.question: Can I commit, push, write README notes, and preserve evidence of work?
checkpoints.whyThisMatters: Unversioned, unshared work isn't professional evidence. This checkpoint verifies your work is real, public, and explainable.
signsOfConfidence: Your commit messages explain intent, not just 'update'.
Your READMEs let a stranger run your code.
You use Git as a safety net, not just a submission mechanism.

checkpoints.question: Can I build reusable components, use state, render lists, create routes, and persist data?
checkpoints.whyThisMatters: React is the interface layer for both Elliot's web app and, via React Native, its mobile app. This is the single most reused skill in the back half of the bootcamp.
signsOfConfidence: You reach for state, not manual DOM manipulation, to make UI change.
You never mutate state directly.
You can explain why a list needs stable keys.

checkpoints.question: Can I create Express routes that return and update JSON data?
checkpoints.whyThisMatters: A frontend without a backend is a demo, not a product. This checkpoint verifies you can build the data layer real apps depend on.
signsOfConfidence: You can design sensible REST routes for a new resource from scratch.
You never trust client input without validating it server-side.
You understand why a server must stay running to serve requests.

checkpoints.question: Can I make an app more mobile-friendly, installable, reliable, and product-ready?
checkpoints.whyThisMatters: Reliability and mobile reach are what make a product trustworthy and usable in the real world, not just on your dev machine.
signsOfConfidence: You validate and handle errors by default, not as an afterthought.
You test at real mobile widths, not just desktop.
You can explain what makes a web app installable.

checkpoints.question: Can I run a React Native/Expo app on my Samsung A70 and connect it to data?
checkpoints.whyThisMatters: This is the checkpoint that proves you're not just a web developer - you can ship on a real device, the platform most users actually carry.
signsOfConfidence: You've run and debugged an app on your own physical phone.
You understand why mobile storage is asynchronous.
You can build multi-screen navigation confidently.

checkpoints.question: Can Elliot V1 run on web/mobile, save notes/tasks, answer from personal data, read basic documents, and connect to a backend?
checkpoints.whyThisMatters: This is the bootcamp's ultimate checkpoint: not 'do you know React' but 'can you ship a real, working, multi-layer product end to end.'
signsOfConfidence: Elliot runs on both web and mobile against a real backend.
You can explain every architectural decision in Elliot V1, including what you deliberately left out.
You'd be comfortable demoing Elliot live to a stranger.

roadmap.roadmapTitle: XcelerateAI 6-Month JavaScript Mobile Ops Bootcamp: Elliot Product Track
roadmap.roadmapShortTitle: XcelerateAI 6-Month JavaScript Mobile Ops Bootcamp: Elliot Product Track
roadmap.targetAudience: Learners with theoretical programming exposure who need to build practical, professional full-stack JavaScript ability across web, backend, and mobile, culminating in a real shipped product (Elliot V1).
roadmap.description: A six-month, project-driven path from JavaScript fundamentals to a working, multi-layer product: a browser-based interface, a Node/Express backend, and a React Native/Expo mobile app, connected into one assistant product (Elliot V1).
learningOutcome: Build interactive, data-driven web interfaces with vanilla JavaScript, the DOM, and React
Design and implement REST APIs and CRUD data flows with Node.js and Express
Ship an installable Progressive Web App and a native-feeling mobile app with React Native/Expo
Connect a web client, a mobile client, and a backend API into one coherent, working product
Debug, test, document, and deploy real software using a professional Git/GitHub workflow
Independently plan and build a full-stack product from an ambiguous idea to a demoable V1

answers.explanation: The launch environment is the setup where JavaScript runs, such as the browser, VS Code, or Node.js. The first JavaScript output is usually console.log(), which helps confirm that the environment is working.
I learnt quite alot this week, building up on what i learnt last week on data types, variables and so on...

Creating and using functions aren't as difficult as I deemed them to be, especially because of the manner in which it is written with javascript.

The ability to input logic without much difficulty or too many syntactical procedures is in of itself an astronomical advantage. I had fun tinkering about with the various capabilities of

reflections.0: This was genuinely fun as I managed to write the code without help after knowing that all i needed was console.log and the writing inside open and closed brackets...
I had already completed these tasks even before the time alloted for the project.

Today's task was much more difficult as I had to figure out that I needed to use conditionals and how to use it too. It was fun eitherways, arranging the code, and figuring out where to put what and also naming the variables to solve the problem presented to me.

having left the command center for quite a while - i was finalising the frontend and Json file improvements, I came back and surprisingly remembered everything I had been doing, perhaps because I was able to repeatedly practice the tasks given to me previously.

I completed the final task with very little intervention or help from external docs.

This project was quite confusing at first, as the requirement to build it was a little bit vague. I didnt know what the output should look like, hence, my difficulty in producing a result aligning with the requirment of the task. 

I however used the assistance or rather, guidance of AI to complete the task. 
I made use of the if-elseif-else conditional, a const, and the creation of the proofSubmitted function (a concept that is still quite vague to me)

This week was infinitely increased in difficulty compared to last week. Functions was a huge jump mainly because I mis interpreted the complexity of the programs, had to think logically and found myself making errors with some principles of function initialization and creation. All-in-all, i see the use of functions and its importance in programming.

The most important point is:
"If your function does more than one task, its probably doing its job wrongly. A function should do only one task at a time."

This week became relatively easy by mission 3. I eventually mastered the concept of parameters, functions and variables - however the logic aspect still leaves much to be wanted. In spite of that, I have improved drastically, writing code from the top of my head, with little or no help from external sources.

1.explanation:
This week was quite eventful. I learnt more about github than i thought i knew, and i will definitely learn even more.

I learnt how to print out variables, manipulate and declare variables using the "let" keyword and finally, using the console.log keyword to print out results onto the terminal.

2.explanation:
Well firstly, it was really fun having to test out different coding keywords and characters, and writing code that was once very tedious for me, and even more tedious to remember.

I constantly used the "let" keyword throughout this week, as it was the unifying data type assignor. It saves me alot of stress in trying to remember the data type and variable type and all that...

i did encounter the "undefined issue" earlier as i forgot that I should've put my string variables into double quotes "". I almost used AI, but then I chose to sit back, observe the error (I figured that I had already faced this before the debugging task of previous assignments), and after careful observation, I figured it out!

i figured out that if I am to write the logic to a code using variables, I better do it right. One small mistake could speel hours of fixing unforseen bugs.

I can rebuild all from a blank file, literally!

3.explanation: I leveraged on my knowledge on the creation and initialisation of variables to write various functions each performing one task each, taking in the parameters (return/result) of previous functions to create new responses and results.
